Users are grouped by rounding their coordinates to nearest 0.2° User A at (48.856, 2.352) → grid cell 48.8_2.4 (cache key) User B at (48.772, 2.421) → same grid cell 48.8_2.4 (same cache key) Both users can get plane data for the area without storing their exact locations anywhere. As you can see, User B falls within the same grid cell initialized by User A, so both users share the same cache entry 48.8_2.4. Any user in this area will use the same entry. After the plane data is retrieved, each user only sees aircraft within a 12 km detection radius centered on their location. This filtering happens on the client side to minimize backend resource usage and keep the system flexible. If a user is near the edge of a grid cell, they might miss planes flying just outside the grid. Corner users could see only a quarter of the surrounding sky. See the diagram below for a better visualization: The green planes (Plane A and Plane C) are cached and fall within the detection radii of their respective users so notifications will be triggered. ✅ The yellow plane (Plane B) is inside the grid cell, so it's cached as well. Users will see it on the page, but no notification will be sent until it enters one of the detection circles. ❌ The white planes (Plane E, Plane D, and Plane F), however, are outside the grid cell and therefore won't be cached, nor will they be shown on the map, even though Plane D is technically within the detection radius of User C. ❌ Now, this is a significant drawback, because it means some users might not receive fully accurate information about nearby planes. And this is exactly where the Bounding Box strategy saves the day. Fetching a slightly larger rectangle ensures everyone gets the full "all-around" view. The backend actually fetches a 50 km × 50 km rectangle around the grid cell center, slightly larger than the grid itself, to ensure full coverage of the area. As you can see, Plane D has just turned green, which means User C will now receive a notification about it. Keep in mind: the bounding box serves a completely different purpose than the grid cell. If a new user appears within the bounding box but outside the existing grid cell, a new grid cell and consequently a new bounding box will be created for them. The bounding box's only job is to ensure that no planes are missed near the edges. Looking at the diagram, you can see that the bounding box doesn't need to be this large, which is fine for now. In future versions of the app, users will be able to adjust their detection radius and making it bigger (or smaller). Clients don't poll the server at fixed intervals. Instead, the server tells each client when to request new data, based on cache freshness. This approach: To calculate the exact distance between a plane and a user, I use the Haversine formula, which measures distance on a sphere. This ensures accurate notifications, even for users near the edge of a grid cell.

synthesized_points: Most software developers spend their working days indoors under artificial lighting, locked to an IDE, staring at screens for hours on end.

By mid-afternoon, the consequences are familiar across the tech community: eye strain, brain fog, fading focus, and a disrupted circadian rhythm that makes quality sleep an uphill battle. For years, I treated this as simply the unavoidable occupational hazard of writing code.
The real issue isn't a lack of discipline or coffee—it's that standard indoor work environments fight against basic human biology.

The human body relies on natural daylight to set its internal circadian clock. But standard office windows filter out the specific daylight wavelengths needed to feel alert. Even sitting right next to a window, indoor lighting is rarely brighter than 400–500 lux—compared to 10,000+ lux outdoors. To the body, sitting inside all day feels like constant twilight, draining energy and throwing off sleep.

And the tech industry's standard answer to developer burnout? Another screen. Wellness apps that demand more typing, habit trackers with endless push notifications, and weather apps that treat sunlight purely as a sunburn hazard.

SunSync is a lightweight open-source daylight timing tool built with a single goal: evaluate local sunlight in under 30 seconds, give you a quick 15-second eyes-free voice brief, lock into a 20-minute outdoor breathing timer, and get you away from your desk into the fresh air.

The Outdoor Breathing Lock — When you tap "I'm going outside", the UI locks into a 20-minute circular breathing timer so you can put your phone away. You focus on the horizon (never staring directly at the sun) and return to your desk refreshed and ready to code.
📡 Interactive OpenAPI Specification: https://sunsync.omar-afifi.com/docs

synthesized_points: If you ask an AI chatbot for movie recommendations or a recipe, a small hallucination is harmless. But if you ask it about the Quran, religious scripture, or classical commentary, getting things wrong is not an option.
When two classical scholars disagree, the model either invents a fake consensus or blends both opinions into a confusing, contradictory mess.
It cites famous books and scholars with total confidence, even when the quote never existed in that book.
Traditional RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) doesn't fix this either, because dumping raw chunks into a prompt still leaves the model free to summarize, blur, and paraphrase whatever it wants.
Quran Sanity Agent is a bilingual (Arabic & English) web research workspace where every single verse, translation, and scholarly commentary is anchored to an immutable record in Sanity.

Verses Are Read, Never Generated — The LLM is never asked to recite or recall Quranic text from memory. Every Ayah displayed in the interface is pulled directly from a verified Sanity document matching the authoritative Tanzil Uthmani 1.1 reference standard.

Scholarly Differences as Structured Data — In classical Islamic exegesis (Tafsir), scholars have debated linguistic nuances and legal rulings for over a thousand years. Instead of hiding these differences, the application structures them into two distinct categories — Contradictory (Ikhtilaf Tadadd): True conflicting positions (e.g., whether the opening Basmalah is counted as a verse of Al-Fatihah). · Complementary (Ikhtilaf Tanawwu'): Multi-faceted meanings that coexist (e.g., whether Al-Asr refers to time itself or the afternoon prayer).

The Evidence Drawer — Every verse and commentary card has an interactive citation badge. Clicking it opens a side drawer showing the exact Sanity Document ID, the physical book locator (chapter, volume, primary URL), and the raw JSON payload straight from the Content Lake.

Honest Evidence Gaps — If you ask a question outside the curated dataset (like modern cryptocurrency rulings), the agent doesn't try to guess or produce an ungrounded opinion. It explicitly reports an Evidence Gap, showing what records it searched and clarifying that no authoritative source is available.
🏛️ Hosted Sanity Studio: https://quran-evidence-studio.sanity.studio/
Zero-Trust Transparency: The Live Evidence Drawer — Inspect real-time Sanity Document IDs, physical book locators, and raw JSON payloads straight from the Content Lake.

Exact Verse Integrity — Query: 2:255 (or switch the UI to Arabic and type البقرة ٢٥٥). · What to look for: Instant retrieval of Ayat al-Kursi with verified Uthmani script and Saheeh International translation. Click the citation badge to view ayah-2-255 in the Evidence Drawer.

Contradictory Divergence — Query: Compare interpretations of Al-Fatiha Basmalah · What to look for: Surfaces the opposing classical positions between Ibn Kathir / Al-Qurtubi vs. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi side-by-side, without the model taking a side or muddying the waters.

Complementary Divergence — Query: Compare interpretations of Al-Asr · What to look for: Shows how Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, and Al-Qurtubi each highlight complementary dimensions of the word (time, human deeds, afternoon prayer).

Semantic Retrieval via Sanity Context MCP — Query: What does the Quran say about justice even against oneself? · What to look for: The agent queries the Sanity Context MCP endpoint, ranks Ayah 4:135 at the top, and provides grounded notes quoting the primary text verbatim.
Web/: Next.js 15 (App Router) interface with full Arabic RTL support and the Sanity Context MCP integration.
Studio/: Sanity Studio v3 with custom Desk Structure and dedicated Islamic hermeneutic schemas.
Scripts/: Verification tools ensuring zero character drift against reference text standards.
How I Used Sanity — This project is built around the idea that an agent is only as reliable as the structure behind its content.
The Content Model (studio/schemaTypes/) — Surah: Core chapter metadata (number, Arabic name, English name, revelation type, verse count).
The Editorial Review Gate — One of the most practical things about Sanity Studio is how easily you can customize the Desk Structure to enforce editorial discipline.

The Editorial Review Gate — In studio/deskStructure.ts, I added a custom "Needs source review" filter: If an editor enters a new claim but forgets the primary book excerpt, the exact source URL, or the reviewer sign-off, Sanity immediately catches it and moves it into this review queue.

The Editorial Review Gate — More importantly, the Next.js agent's GROQ queries strictly filter for reviewStatus in ["source_checked", "reviewed"]. If a claim hasn't passed the editorial gate, the AI agent is physically unable to see it or use it in an answer.
The Grounding Rule — The agent never relies solely on the LLM's summary. It uses those document IDs to re-fetch the raw records directly from the Content Lake.

Verbatim Quotation Enforcement — If the model generates an explanatory note, the application validates that the note quotes words directly from the retrieved source text. If it fails this check, the UI falls back to displaying the raw verified excerpt.

all_paragraphs: When I first opened the Sanity Challenge announcement, one sentence in the Path One brief immediately grabbed my attention:
"Build anything that needs an answer it can't afford to get wrong."

If you ask an AI chatbot for movie recommendations or a recipe, a small hallucination is harmless. But if you ask it about the Quran, religious scripture, or classical commentary, getting things wrong is not an option.
Traditional RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) doesn't fix this either, because dumping raw chunks into a prompt still leaves the model free to summarize, blur, and paraphrase whatever it wants.

I wanted to see what happens when you treat the problem differently: what if the AI literally cannot generate Quranic text? What if the agent only has access to verified, structured records in Sanity, and conflicting historical opinions are modeled cleanly as data rather than smoothed over?
Quran Sanity Agent is a bilingual (Arabic & English) web research workspace where every single verse, translation, and scholarly commentary is anchored to an immutable record in Sanity.
Inspect real-time Sanity Document IDs, physical book locators, and raw JSON payloads straight from the Content Lake.
This project is built around the idea that an agent is only as reliable as the structure behind its content.
Instead of generic blog or article schemas, Sanity Studio manages structured Quranic and classical commentary data:
One of the most practical things about Sanity Studio is how easily you can customize the Desk Structure to enforce editorial discipline.

In studio/deskStructure.ts, I added a custom "Needs source review" filter: If an editor enters a new claim but forgets the primary book excerpt, the exact source URL, or the reviewer sign-off, Sanity immediately catches it and moves it into this review queue.

More importantly, the Next.js agent's GROQ queries strictly filter for reviewStatus in ["source_checked", "reviewed"]. If a claim hasn't passed the editorial gate, the AI agent is physically unable to see it or use it in an answer.
While exact verse numbers (e.g. 2:255) are resolved instantly via deterministic GROQ queries, thematic questions (e.g. "What does the Quran say about justice?") require semantic understanding.
To handle this, I pointed Sanity Context at the imported library of 21,398 chunks and enabled Content Lake embeddings:
The solution to AI hallucination in high-stakes domains isn't "better prompts" or larger models. It's structured content.

When you treat texts as unstructured strings dumped into a vector database, the AI is always one step away from fabricating an answer. But when you model your domain properly—distinguishing chapters from verses, authorities from editions, and consensus from disagreement—the AI stops guessing and starts acting as an interface to verified knowledge.

Sanity was uniquely suited for this: having schemas, the Content Lake, GROQ, and the Context MCP in one unified ecosystem meant I could build a zero-hallucination agent that remains completely transparent with every answer it gives.
Check out the live project at quran-sanity.omar-afifi.com and explore the code on GitHub.

https://dev.to/omarafifi/the-ghost-in-th.overview: While working on a major upgrade for my personal portfolio (Check it out here: Live Portfolio Link | GitHub Repo), I built a feature called the Theme Showcase. When a user first loads the homepage, a slick View Transitions API animation sweeps across the screen, temporarily switching the site to one of my custom showcase themes (like "Obsidian" or "Midnight"), before gracefully sweeping back to their chosen default theme. takeaways: 🐛 Bug Fix — Soon after deploying, I noticed a terrifying, chaotic bug. Sometimes, I would open the website and quickly switch to another tab to check an email, or minimize the browser window completely. When I switched back...
💻 Code — Here is the exact code change we made to exorcise the ghost. (You can view the full fix in this GitHub Commit)

Phase 1: The Misdiagnosis — The AI analyzed the code and thought the animation feature itself was the bug (assuming it was just annoying the user). So, it enthusiastically offered a "fix" by completely disabling the showcase animation function!

Phase 2: The Deep Dive — AI: "When you save, the dev server refreshes the page. The animation starts, switches to the showcase theme, and then returns. You are just manually refreshing before the 1.7 seconds finish, trapping yourself in a loop! Just wait 1.7 seconds."
synthesized_points: 🐛 Bug Fix — Soon after deploying, I noticed a terrifying, chaotic bug. Sometimes, I would open the website and quickly switch to another tab to check an email, or minimize the browser window completely. When I switched back...

🐛 Bug Fix — Instead of my beautiful default theme, the website was permanently stuck on one of the other showcase themes! The animation had frozen mid-way, leaving the site in an awkward intermediate state. While the website was still fully functional and I could manually fix it by selecting my original theme from the dropdown menu, it was a terrible first impression for a professional portfolio. It was as if a ghost had possessed the CSS.

🐛 Bug Fix — My first instinct? Smash the refresh button. Refreshing would actually fix the glitch and play the animation perfectly—but only if I stayed patiently on the tab and watched it finish! If I refreshed and immediately switched tabs again, the ghost would return.
💻 Code — Here is the exact code change we made to exorcise the ghost. (You can view the full fix in this GitHub Commit)

State Management on Visibility Change — I added a visibilitychange event listener. If the user navigates away, we instantly cancel the sequence and forcefully restore the original theme to prevent intermediate states.

Error Handling for the View Transitions API — The core issue was that browsers forcefully abort the startViewTransition when a tab is hidden to save battery. This caused the transition.ready Promise to reject. Because there was no .catch() block, the unhandled rejection caused the entire async sequence to hang permanently. By wrapping the transition in a try/catch and adding a .catch(() => resolve()) handler, we guarantee that the execution flow always continues gracefully, even if the browser interrupts it.

🤖 Best Use of Google AI — I couldn't figure out why this bug was only happening sometimes, and no errors were showing up in the console. So, I turned to my trusty pair programmer: Google AI integrated within the Antigravity IDE.

🤖 Best Use of Google AI — What's really cool about my workflow is that I chat with my AI agent completely casually in Arabic. It feels incredibly natural, like brainstorming with a senior engineer sitting right next to me. But debugging with AI isn't always a "one-shot" magic trick. It’s an iterative journey.

🤖 Best Use of Google AI — (Note: I interact with my AI agent natively in Arabic! For this post, I have translated our debugging conversation. I've kept the original Arabic screenshots on hand just in case the judges want to see them!)
Phase 1: The Misdiagnosis — Me: "I have another issue. Sometimes the theme changes to dark suddenly and weird things happen. I don't know what it is."

Phase 1: The Misdiagnosis — The AI analyzed the code and thought the animation feature itself was the bug (assuming it was just annoying the user). So, it enthusiastically offered a "fix" by completely disabling the showcase animation function!

Phase 1: The Misdiagnosis — Me: "Bro, no, you misunderstood! The animation at the beginning is natural and fine. What's NOT natural is leaving the website open, going to another tab, and coming back to find it permanently stuck on a new theme."

Phase 2: The Deep Dive — Once I steered the AI in the right direction, it immediately dug into the mechanics of tab-switching. It realized that modern browsers aggressively pause requestAnimationFrame when a tab goes to the background.
Phase 2: The Deep Dive — The AI wrote the visibilitychange listener, but then we ran into another issue when I was testing it locally with my dev server.
Phase 2: The Deep Dive — Me: "Why does it open on a different theme every time I hit save in my editor? I have to manually refresh to get my original theme back."

Phase 2: The Deep Dive — AI: "When you save, the dev server refreshes the page. The animation starts, switches to the showcase theme, and then returns. You are just manually refreshing before the 1.7 seconds finish, trapping yourself in a loop! Just wait 1.7 seconds."

Phase 3: The "Aha!" Moment — Me: "Bro, I'm not rushing. I open it, find it on a new theme, and it is completely STUCK on it. This causes problems if the user goes to another tab. Focus well, think carefully, and take your time."

Phase 3: The "Aha!" Moment — It didn't just hand me a snippet of code; it provided a masterclass on browser mechanics. It analyzed the View Transitions API behavior and uncovered the true root cause: to save battery and resources, modern browsers aggressively throttle or abort animations when a tab is hidden. This aggressive optimization was causing the transition.ready promise to reject silently, which hung the entire async sequence because it lacked a .catch() block.

Phase 3: The "Aha!" Moment — Thanks to Google AI in the Antigravity IDE, I didn't just fix a bug—I learned exactly why the browser was behaving that way under the hood. It transformed a frustrating debugging session into a profound learning experience about advanced JavaScript APIs and browser rendering mechanics. This is exactly what the future of pair programming looks like!

https://dev.to/georgekobaidze/promise-de.overview: The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you love the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.
takeaways: AWS VPC From Scratch: Building Your Own Private Network Inside AWS — My take: One of the most useful and practical articles I've read in a while. As someone who uses AWS frequently, it's easy to forget the details over time, and this is a great refresher on how VPCs, subnets, security groups, and NACLs fit together. The analogies make it all stick.

SQL Common Table Expressions and Window functions — Why they picked it: His first real dip into tech writing, and he spent the time digging into the database to make sure everything he wrote was fact.

Gnoke POC: Proof of concept — My take: I love the philosophy behind this. "Deploying 14 microservices to save a note" made me laugh, because it's painfully accurate. Complexity often looks smart from a distance, but simplicity is what survives. Good architecture starts with decomposition, not with tools.

I Tried Pair Programming With Three Different AI Tools For a Month — My take: The idea that AI shifts engineering work rather than removing it is spot on. Reviewing diffs, checking assumptions, and breaking tasks into smaller pieces have become core skills. And step 7, asking the AI to challenge its own solution, is such a simple habit, yet it catches a lot.
synthesized_points: The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you love the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.
I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.
Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.
That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: "Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"
Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.
The longest read — 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100.
The oldest exhibit — published in March 2020.
Zero reactions — 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists.
How to Tour the Hall — 🚪 The Welcome Desk: where every visitor should start
Why they picked it: It made it onto DEV's official community resources page and earned a badge for it.

My take: If I'd had something like this when I first joined DEV, I'd have been a lot more active from day one. It's the perfect first stop for anyone new here, which is exactly why it's the first stop of this tour.
A Builder in Paris: Do Devs Dream of Électrique Chats? — Why they picked it: Written after walking away from the computer on vacation and realizing there was an idea worth coming back to.

A Builder in Paris: Do Devs Dream of Électrique Chats? — My take: I loved this one from the first few sentences, because it mentions rainy, cold days, and those are my favorite. That's when I feel most alive. It also reminded me of my own work-to-travel switch: a few hours before a flight, I recorded a 20-minute video, only to find out it had no sound at all. Sometimes the best thing you can do for your work is step away from it.
Coding Without Pressure: How Slowing Down Helped Me Learn Faster — Why they picked it: So many people related to it, and it got over 13K views in less than 3 days.

Coding Without Pressure: How Slowing Down Helped Me Learn Faster — My take: It's brief, but it's packed with painfully relatable stuff. As a junior engineer, I tried to learn everything by heart, because I thought that's how real developers worked. Then reality punched me in the face. Just consuming information is pretending to progress. Real progress comes when you're in motion, with 10 bugs to fix and zero clue how, and you still have to figure it out.

A Letter to Jobseekers: Don't Give Up! — My take: Relatable for pretty much everyone in a field that can be way too tough and unforgiving. I've had my own share of rock bottom, which back then felt like the end of my career. Looking back, I'd never have achieved half of what I have without it. Learning to turn bad situations to your advantage is a superpower.
Dreams & Cheers — Why they picked it: It's kind of his first post, and it's about dreams that are still waiting to be fulfilled.

Dreams & Cheers — My take: The key quote: "I feel I do not belong there, but it is too late..." You don't know what's behind the door until you step inside. I admire anyone with the courage to stick around where they "don't belong", only to find out it's their natural habitat.

The Most Painful Career Lesson My Best Job Taught Me — My take: I love that someone picked an article titled "The Most Painful Career Lesson My Best Job Taught Me" as their favorite. It shows you're not trying to forget bad experiences, you embrace them. Not everyone can do that. The more experience you gain, the more you realize there's no such thing as a bad experience in a career. Bad ones teach you far more than good ones.

The Code That Started It All ! — My take: What a story! Everyone's story of how they started programming is special, but some are more special than others. As a fellow gamer, engineer, and introvert, I related to a lot of it. For the record, my own first software code was in C++, 20 years ago, in Borland C++. I was 11. Simpler times.

The Stack Nobody Picks Might Be the One That Picks You — My take: As a .NET developer with C# as my primary language for 10 years, this one hit home. Would I pick a different stack if I could go back? Absolutely NOT! Web apps, desktop apps, games, mobile apps, back-end services, you name it. Learn one language, and you can build almost anything. And as long as there are enough jobs out there, you only need one.

My take: I totally understand the frustration. No matter how great your project is, without backing or marketing it rarely takes off right away. That's not a reason to give up, it's learning material: get to know your audience, understand the demand, and try again. Every failure is a lesson in disguise.

Turns out that's not a strategy, it's a prayer. What I appreciate most is that this isn't a compliance checklist, every point explains who it actually helps and why. It's listed at 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100. Worth every one of them.

A class doesn't inherit from an interface, it implements it, and that difference is gigantic. Months into my first job, I still didn't get why we needed interfaces at all. Every tutorial said "loose coupling is good." Sure, but WHY? This article answers exactly that. And the "Badass Prince" badge analogy cracked me up. One of the best in the whole thread. 🔥

Your Talk Is Not a University Lecture — There's one trap beginners sometimes fall into. A 30-minute or even 45-minute conference presentation isn't a deep dive or a workshop. You don't need to transfer every piece of knowledge you have into the audience's brains. They won't remember it all anyway.
synthesized_points: Recently, a few people have asked me what it's actually like to speak at tech conferences. How do you get accepted? What does preparation look like? And what happens behind the scenes? So I decided to write about it. And let me warn you: the reality isn't always pretty. In fact, after hearing about my experiences, one person has already put their conference-speaking plans on hold indefinitely. 😅

Because conferences aren't just about getting on stage and having fun. They're also about rejected abstracts, endless preparation, stress, and logistics. And is it actually worth it? Let's find out! 😉

One little disclaimer: everything I'm about to share is based on my own experiences and observations. Other speakers might have completely different perspectives, and I'd love to hear them in the comments!

First, a Little About My Conference Experience — Before we start, let me briefly tell you about my conference "achievements," so you know where I'm coming from. I gave various talks and workshops around 2019, then took a break for several years to focus on my professional development, occasionally running a workshop here and there.
First, a Little About My Conference Experience — I even had to turn down one invitation because I simply couldn't fit it into my schedule anymore. :(I still regret it!

First, a Little About My Conference Experience — I got accepted to some through CFPs, was invited to others, and got a few opportunities partly through connections (for example, because another speaker remembered me from a previous conference).

First, a Little About My Conference Experience — I'm not a keynote speaker. I often speak on additional tracks or in smaller rooms, and I'm perfectly fine with that. Actually, I think that's what makes my perspective interesting. I'm not a conference veteran with ten years of experience whom organizers are fighting to book.

First, a Little About My Conference Experience — And while I feel pretty confident about blogging these days, conference speaking still gives me a massive case of impostor syndrome. Especially since English isn't my native language. I always think nobody will ever invite me again. And somehow, people keep inviting me. 😅

Getting Accepted: The Wonderful World of CFPs — If you're not the face of a huge tech company, the maintainer of a famous library, or some kind of tech celebrity, your main option is to apply through a CFP (Call for Papers). Most major conferences accept talk proposals, so you just need to check their websites for submission deadlines.
Getting Accepted: The Wonderful World of CFPs — Sounds simple, right? Well, if only conference organizers were sitting there, eagerly waiting for our submissions!

Getting Accepted: The Wonderful World of CFPs — Let's say a conference has 20 speaking slots. That doesn't mean organizers will select 20 people from the CFP. Quite a few slots might go to invited speakers — well-known names who help sell tickets. Others might go to sponsors. And who knows who else! When hundreds of submissions compete for the remaining places, your chances aren't exactly amazing.

Getting Accepted: The Wonderful World of CFPs — Rejections are completely normal, and they don't necessarily tell you much about the quality of your abstract. Your topic might have been great but didn't fit the agenda, or the organizers decided it wasn't relevant to their audience.

Getting Accepted: The Wonderful World of CFPs — But let's not fool ourselves, either. Your topic might simply have been weak, and submitting it twenty times won't magically make it better. You can ask organizers for feedback, but they're under no obligation to provide it.
How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — As someone who has lost quite a few CFP battles but managed to win a few as well, I can offer some advice.

How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — First, look at your abstract from the organizers' perspective. They're not selecting you just to make you happy. You need to bring something valuable to their conference.

How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — If you're not famous enough to sell tickets just by having your name on the agenda (and I'm guessing you're not, unless you're just reading this out of curiosity), you need an exceptionally interesting topic. Something original that hasn't already been submitted by 20 other people.

How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — Ideally, a case study from your work or personal projects, or a fresh perspective on a familiar subject. Your topic should be original, but not too niche, either. After all, people still need to be interested in it.

How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — For example, I've traveled to a few conferences with a talk about WebGPU, but I presented it more broadly as "Your Browser Is a Compute Platform." It was a big-picture talk about what browsers can do these days, including running LLMs directly in the browser. Because if I'd submitted something like "Introduction to WebGPU with Shaders," I'm pretty sure nobody would have cared.

How to Make Your Talk Stand Out — Spend some time working on your abstract, too. Ask yourself: what will attendees actually take away from this talk? This will also help you prepare the narrative later. And who knows? You might realize your talk isn't particularly useful in its current form and that you should rethink the approach.

The Catch: Nobody Knows If You Can Actually Speak — Now, here's another problem. You might have a fantastic topic and a beautifully written abstract, but if you have absolutely no speaking experience, getting accepted will be much harder — especially at prestigious conferences.

The Catch: Nobody Knows If You Can Actually Speak — Again, put yourself in the organizers' shoes. How do they know whether someone who's never stood on a stage can handle the stress, deliver an interesting presentation, and finish on time? (By the way, finishing one minute early is much better than finishing five minutes late.)

all_paragraphs: So you want to be a conference speaker? Are you sure?

Recently, a few people have asked me what it's actually like to speak at tech conferences. How do you get accepted? What does preparation look like? And what happens behind the scenes? So I decided to write about it. And let me warn you: the reality isn't always pretty. In fact, after hearing about my experiences, one person has already put their conference-speaking plans on hold indefinitely. 😅

Because conferences aren't just about getting on stage and having fun. They're also about rejected abstracts, endless preparation, stress, and logistics. And is it actually worth it? Let's find out! 😉

One little disclaimer: everything I'm about to share is based on my own experiences and observations. Other speakers might have completely different perspectives, and I'd love to hear them in the comments!

Before we start, let me briefly tell you about my conference "achievements," so you know where I'm coming from. I gave various talks and workshops around 2019, then took a break for several years to focus on my professional development, occasionally running a workshop here and there.
I even had to turn down one invitation because I simply couldn't fit it into my schedule anymore. :(I still regret it!
I got accepted to some through CFPs, was invited to others, and got a few opportunities partly through connections (for example, because another speaker remembered me from a previous conference).

I'm not a keynote speaker. I often speak on additional tracks or in smaller rooms, and I'm perfectly fine with that. Actually, I think that's what makes my perspective interesting. I'm not a conference veteran with ten years of experience whom organizers are fighting to book.

And while I feel pretty confident about blogging these days, conference speaking still gives me a massive case of impostor syndrome. Especially since English isn't my native language. I always think nobody will ever invite me again. And somehow, people keep inviting me. 😅
Okay, so how do you actually get accepted as a conference speaker?

If you're not the face of a huge tech company, the maintainer of a famous library, or some kind of tech celebrity, your main option is to apply through a CFP (Call for Papers). Most major conferences accept talk proposals, so you just need to check their websites for submission deadlines.
Sounds simple, right? Well, if only conference organizers were sitting there, eagerly waiting for our submissions!

Let's say a conference has 20 speaking slots. That doesn't mean organizers will select 20 people from the CFP. Quite a few slots might go to invited speakers — well-known names who help sell tickets. Others might go to sponsors. And who knows who else! When hundreds of submissions compete for the remaining places, your chances aren't exactly amazing.

Rejections are completely normal, and they don't necessarily tell you much about the quality of your abstract. Your topic might have been great but didn't fit the agenda, or the organizers decided it wasn't relevant to their audience.

But let's not fool ourselves, either. Your topic might simply have been weak, and submitting it twenty times won't magically make it better. You can ask organizers for feedback, but they're under no obligation to provide it.
As someone who has lost quite a few CFP battles but managed to win a few as well, I can offer some advice.
First, look at your abstract from the organizers' perspective. They're not selecting you just to make you happy. You need to bring something valuable to their conference.

If you're not famous enough to sell tickets just by having your name on the agenda (and I'm guessing you're not, unless you're just reading this out of curiosity), you need an exceptionally interesting topic. Something original that hasn't already been submitted by 20 other people.

Ideally, a case study from your work or personal projects, or a fresh perspective on a familiar subject. Your topic should be original, but not too niche, either. After all, people still need to be interested in it.

For example, I've traveled to a few conferences with a talk about WebGPU, but I presented it more broadly as "Your Browser Is a Compute Platform." It was a big-picture talk about what browsers can do these days, including running LLMs directly in the browser. Because if I'd submitted something like "Introduction to WebGPU with Shaders," I'm pretty sure nobody would have cared.

Spend some time working on your abstract, too. Ask yourself: what will attendees actually take away from this talk? This will also help you prepare the narrative later. And who knows? You might realize your talk isn't particularly useful in its current form and that you should rethink the approach.

Now, here's another problem. You might have a fantastic topic and a beautifully written abstract, but if you have absolutely no speaking experience, getting accepted will be much harder — especially at prestigious conferences.

Again, put yourself in the organizers' shoes. How do they know whether someone who's never stood on a stage can handle the stress, deliver an interesting presentation, and finish on time? (By the way, finishing one minute early is much better than finishing five minutes late.)
Blogging or making YouTube videos can help, because they at least demonstrate your storytelling skills. And of course, some conferences happily accept first-time speakers.

But if you're struggling to get accepted anywhere, consider starting with a local meetup. There's usually less competition, and you'll have a speaking engagement to put on your CV. 😉 The more you speak, the better you become, which improves your chances of getting accepted in the future.
Okay, you've been accepted! Is this where the fame and fortune begin? Hahahaha. I seriously doubt it.

People often ask me whether conference speakers get paid. Well, some do, especially famous keynote speakers who can command speaking fees. But if you're a regular speaker accepted through a CFP, you probably shouldn't expect payment. At least, that's been my experience. I know there are exceptions, so feel free to correct me!

Conferences often cover travel and accommodation, but read their policies carefully. Personally, I always make sure those costs are covered. I mean, okay, I might not earn anything, but I'm certainly not going to pay out of my own pocket for the privilege of speaking. So check this before submitting your proposal.
Sometimes your employer will cover your expenses if they consider your appearance good publicity for the company. But again, make sure that's actually the case before committing to the trip.
So, how much work does it take to prepare a conference talk? Well, it depends!

While comparing outputs, I kept noticing that the hardest parts weren't vocabulary. They were structure: things Georgian simply doesn't encode that English requires, and the other way around.
And because I'm a developer, my brain immediately filed these under one label: language features. Some features make life easier, some make it harder, and almost all of them are trade-offs.

I'll compare English and Georgian, since those are the only two languages I know (for now, German is in progress). I love both of them, and both are beautiful in their own way. But they couldn't be more different. Georgian has its own alphabet, Mkhedruli, with 33 letters and no uppercase or lowercase in everyday writing. Yes, my native language is case-insensitive by design. We don't really need casing at all.

Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them) — English marks whether a noun is definite (a specific thing the listener already knows about) or indefinite (something new or non-specific). That's the whole job of the versus a/an.

Feature #1: Articles (or the Lack of Them) — No articles. None. Zero. Null. Undefined. The listener figures out definiteness from context: what was mentioned before, word order, and the situation itself. The first "bus" is obviously new information, the second one is obviously the same bus.

The Upside — It's simpler. Fewer words to say and write, and nothing to choose. You never have to stop and think about which article goes where, which is famously one of the hardest parts of English for people whose native languages don't have articles.

The Downside — And here's where it connects back to my AI research: when a model translates Georgian into English, it has to insert information that wasn't in the source. Every "a" and "the" in the output is a guess. Usually a good one, but still a guess.
Natural gender — pronouns reflect the actual gender of a person. That's English.
Grammatical gender — every noun belongs to a class, including spoons, tables, and the moon. That's Italian, German, and many others.

English: He, She, and It — English has he/him/his, she/her/hers, it/its. That's as far as it goes, and it mostly follows reality: people get he or she, a table is "it". (Except ships, which are sometimes "she" for reasons sailors would have to explain.)
Italian: Two Genders, Every Noun — La mano (hand) is feminine, despite ending in -o

German: Three Genders — Three pieces of cutlery, three genders. It gets better: das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter, because the diminutive suffix -chen always makes a word neuter. Grammar beats biology. And the sun and moon? die Sonne is feminine and der Mond is masculine, the exact opposite of Italian. If gender were logical, the two languages would at least agree on the sky.

German: Three Genders — I recently started learning German, and honestly, der/die/das is the hardest part for me. The standard advice is to never learn a noun without its article, and now I understand why.

Georgian: Zero Genders — When I was a kid and started learning other languages, this was the weirdest thing of all. Why on earth are words divided by gender? That was absolute nonsense to me. Because in Georgian, there's no gender. None. Zero. Not even for people.

https://dev.to/pahorton/i-got-tired-of-c.overview: Hi! I'm Paul and I work as a postdoc in an astrophysics lab as a systems engineer. One of the regular texts I get from my PI is "can you check the pressure on the cryocooler." Our cryocooler, nicknamed Mountain Dewar, is essentially a big cylinder where we test sensitive detectors for space exploration. Our lab moved recently so we're testing Mountain Dewar in a new space after being in retirement for years.
takeaways: The Backstory — Our way of doing this is a multimeter connected to a pressure sensor, where values from 0 to 10V are converted into Torr based on a table in the manual. Because it's just a multimeter, we don't have live pressure data and have to run our tests on a Friday and then check back on Monday to check if it worked.

Formula files — <name>.txt, line 1 = unit, line 2 = expression in V (e.g. degC / V * 100). Functions: sqrt, log, ln, log10, log2, exp, abs, sin, cos tan, asin, acos, atan, pow, min, max, round; constants pi, e. Invalid files are skipped.
Hypertables — the readings table is partitioned by time. The Pi writes to it directly and buffers readings in memory if the network drops.
Continuous aggregates — a one-minute rollup serves graphs of 6 hours or longer, and it matches the raw data to within 0.012 V.
synthesized_points: The Backstory — Hi! I'm Paul and I work as a postdoc in an astrophysics lab as a systems engineer. One of the regular texts I get from my PI is "can you check the pressure on the cryocooler." Our cryocooler, nicknamed Mountain Dewar, is essentially a big cylinder where we test sensitive detectors for space exploration. Our lab moved recently so we're testing Mountain Dewar in a new space after being in retirement for years.

The Backstory — As part of the testing, we got a great deal on a vacuum pump and a bunch of used vacuum parts off eBay that we're trying ensure hold a seal. This means we pump down the cryocooler, taking out all of the air, and then monitor the pressure over time.

The Backstory — Our way of doing this is a multimeter connected to a pressure sensor, where values from 0 to 10V are converted into Torr based on a table in the manual. Because it's just a multimeter, we don't have live pressure data and have to run our tests on a Friday and then check back on Monday to check if it worked.

The Backstory — Myself and a grad student decided to test the capabilities of the lab by building a Voltmeter PCB with a spare Raspberry Pi we had in the lab. He designed a board with a two channel ADC with a voltage differential that we were able to connect to the Pi to give us values from 0 to 12V. We realized that monitoring the pressure wasn't the only thing we had to do in the lab so we made it versatile enough to monitor whatever we wanted.
The Backstory — Once we had a board built and the capabilities of reading voltages, I knew there was more I could do to truly make my life easier.

I was absolutely shocked at how quickly Copilot was able to take my test code for reading the ADCs to creating a working UI on the OLED. I began asking it to add a settings menu with the little joystick and buttons and it was able to do it almost flawlessly. At this point, my PI's request to have a gauge on top of the Cryocooler was done but I realized I could go so much further
Making it Live — /neo Neo Brutalist with colors matching Mountain Dewar
PaHorton / pi_voltmeter — CM4 + ADS1115 (2 channels, single-ended A0/A1) + Adafruit 128x64 OLED bonnet.

This was built with Copilot using a Python application running on a Raspberry Pi to pull data from an ADC, provide a live display on an OLED, and stream data to a TimescaleDB table on TigerData Cloud.
The front end is Flask, FastAPI, and Tailwind CSS for theming. For rendering live data I'm using Chart.js and pulling data from TigerData with the help of their time_bucket and make_interval systems.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter? — We wanted to make this system open source as other labs can very easily have use cases for this. Our PCB is available by request and all of the code is located on GitHub so anyone can easily deploy this for their own lab.

The Lazy Payoff — The day after we got it up and running, my PI asked me to turn off the vacuum pump and give him updates on if it's holding pressure. I was able to just share the website with him and he could monitor it himself without me having to go check it every few hours, instantly giving me the freedom to stay at my desk as we watch the pressure increase.
Hypertables — the readings table is partitioned by time. The Pi writes to it directly and buffers readings in memory if the network drops.
Continuous aggregates — a one-minute rollup serves graphs of 6 hours or longer, and it matches the raw data to within 0.012 V.
Compression and retention policies — data is compressed after one day and dropped after 90 days.
all_paragraphs: Hi! I'm Paul and I work as a postdoc in an astrophysics lab as a systems engineer. One of the regular texts I get from my PI is "can you check the pressure on the cryocooler." Our cryocooler, nicknamed Mountain Dewar, is essentially a big cylinder where we test sensitive detectors for space exploration. Our lab moved recently so we're testing Mountain Dewar in a new space after being in retirement for years.

As part of the testing, we got a great deal on a vacuum pump and a bunch of used vacuum parts off eBay that we're trying ensure hold a seal. This means we pump down the cryocooler, taking out all of the air, and then monitor the pressure over time.

Our way of doing this is a multimeter connected to a pressure sensor, where values from 0 to 10V are converted into Torr based on a table in the manual. Because it's just a multimeter, we don't have live pressure data and have to run our tests on a Friday and then check back on Monday to check if it worked.

Myself and a grad student decided to test the capabilities of the lab by building a Voltmeter PCB with a spare Raspberry Pi we had in the lab. He designed a board with a two channel ADC with a voltage differential that we were able to connect to the Pi to give us values from 0 to 12V. We realized that monitoring the pressure wasn't the only thing we had to do in the lab so we made it versatile enough to monitor whatever we wanted.
Once we had a board built and the capabilities of reading voltages, I knew there was more I could do to truly make my life easier.

Starting with a clean OS on a Raspberry Pi 4B and our new PCB, I began working on the software. Initially this was a task I planned on giving to a prospective new undergrad in our lab but after they were unable to join the group, I decided to see what GitHub Copilot was able to accomplish for a hardware project. I found an Adafruit OLED bonnet that fit nicely on top of the PCB and gave us the ability to get a quick visual for the channels without needing to pull up a monitor.

I was absolutely shocked at how quickly Copilot was able to take my test code for reading the ADCs to creating a working UI on the OLED. I began asking it to add a settings menu with the little joystick and buttons and it was able to do it almost flawlessly. At this point, my PI's request to have a gauge on top of the Cryocooler was done but I realized I could go so much further

My test on if this could be accomplished was done but I realized I could go further. TigerData was a tool I was curious about because most of my work revolves around time series data. Given I had a sensor spitting out constant voltages, TimescaleDB, was the obvious choice. TimescaleDB has the ability to natively give me summarization of data so I can more easily query it.

From there, I connected the Pi to the internet and have it stream data from the device to the TigerData Cloud. Given it's a relatively small stream, the free tier is perfect for my use case. I then had Copilot build out a simple web interface for the device. Finally, I hosted it all on Vercel.
Once I got it all up and running, I decided to have some fun with it. Check out some of these easter egg themes

Then I started wondering: what if I were in his place?
I have worked in QA for 15 years. If I carried all those testing habits into an extreme situation, what would my survival rate be?
My advantage is that a QA engineer rarely trusts a happy path just because somebody says it should work.
Deliver the only copy of a critical item into a city that is clearly falling apart. The environment is unknown. The recipient may be offline. There is no backup route.
Without the “you must be as dedicated as the protagonist” rule, the movie might end in ten minutes. I would return the ticket with this comment:
Preconditions are incomplete. The recipient is unreachable. The production environment is unstable. Release blocked.
Unfortunately, our rules say I still have to continue.

This is where testing experience might help. One strange event can be random. Two might require investigation. But when the roads, people, communications, and infrastructure all fail at the same time, a senior QA should recognize a systemic failure.
The answer is not to keep following the original route. Pause that path. Isolate the risk. Find a safer alternative. Then continue the mission.
I would not casually bring a strangely behaving person into my only vehicle.
That would be the survival equivalent of connecting unvalidated, high-risk input directly to the only production environment that still works.
I would not assume that something is permanently dead just because it fell over once. I would also avoid putting all hope into one sample, one laboratory, one vehicle, or one person.
Every critical process without a backup is just waiting for a sufficiently unlucky day.
Testing experience might help me spot danger earlier, challenge bad assumptions, and stop a broken flow. But it cannot solve fitness, luck, limited resources, or unknown biological monsters.
Of course, being a tester does not automatically make someone good at survival.

I've been working on a text editor called Slate, which has been a really interesting learning experience for me.
One thing I hadn't given much thought to before was what actually happens when you save a file while you're still editing it.
I mean, saving a file sounds pretty simple, right? Write the contents to disk, mark it as saved, done.

The file being written contains the older content, but the editor now has newer changes. So if the save finishes and the editor clears the unsaved indicator, it's basically telling the user everything is saved when it isn't.

Now, AI could have just implemented all of that for me. I could have tested the save button, seen that it worked, and moved on with my life.

I had to study all of this for my Deep Learning exam. Two 50-page PDFs full of academic examples like "Recommend science-fiction books" and "Convert 0°C to Fahrenheit." Technically correct. Practically useless. Nobody is opening ChatGPT to convert Celsius.
So here's the version I wish those PDFs had been — every technique from my syllabus, explained with examples you'll actually use as a developer.
Zero-Shot Prompting — What it is: You ask the AI something directly. No examples. No context. No hand-holding. Just the question.
Zero-Shot Prompting — "Explain the difference between git rebase and git merge in 3 sentences."

Zero-Shot Prompting — You're already doing this. Every time you paste an error into ChatGPT with zero context and pray — that's zero-shot prompting. It works great for questions the model has seen a million times. It falls apart the moment your problem is even slightly niche.
Zero-Shot Prompting — When to use it: Quick lookups, syntax questions, "what does X do" queries. Anything where the AI's pre-trained knowledge is enough.
Zero-Shot Prompting — When it fails: The moment your question involves YOUR codebase, YOUR architecture, or anything the model hasn't been trained on. That's when you need the next one.
Few-Shot Prompting — What it is: You show the AI 2-5 examples of what you want, then let it figure out the pattern and apply it to a new input.
Few-Shot Prompting — Feat: add user authentication with JWT fix: resolve null pointer in payment service refactor: extract validation logic into middleware
Few-Shot Prompting — Now write a commit message for: I added rate limiting to the API endpoints.
Few-Shot Prompting — The model picks up your prefix convention (feat:, fix:, refactor:), your sentence casing, your level of detail — without you having to explain any of it.

Few-Shot Prompting — Another real use: You're converting an old API response format to a new one. Show 3 examples of old → new, paste the 4th old response, and let the model transform it. Saves you from writing a throwaway script.
Few-Shot Prompting — When to use it: Consistent formatting, style matching, repetitive transformations. Anytime you're thinking "I need to do this same thing 40 more times."
Chain-of-Thought Prompting — What it is: You ask the AI to work through a problem systematically — step by step — instead of jumping straight to a conclusion.

Chain-of-Thought Prompting — Without "step by step," the AI might just say "the function looks fine." With it, the AI will trace through edge cases: "If discount is passed as a string like '10%', the multiplication produces NaN, which propagates through the calculation..."

Chain-of-Thought Prompting — Asking for a step-by-step breakdown doesn't necessarily reveal the model's actual internal reasoning — but it does force a more inspectable answer: stated assumptions, intermediate checks, edge cases considered, and only then a conclusion. That structure is what makes the mistakes easier to catch.

Chain-of-Thought Prompting — This is exactly how I tracked down a clients.matchAll() race condition in one of my project's service workers. Copilot's first answer was confident and completely wrong. Asking it to walk through the event lifecycle step by step — not "fix this," but "trace what happens between these two events" — is what actually surfaced the timing bug.

Chain-of-Thought Prompting — When to use it: Debugging, code reviews, any question where the reasoning matters more than the answer. If you've ever gotten a confident but completely wrong answer from an AI — this is probably what was missing.
Tree-of-Thought Prompting — What it is: Instead of following one reasoning path, the AI explores multiple paths in parallel. Chain-of-thought is a straight line. Tree-of-thought is a decision tree.
Tree-of-Thought Prompting — List the environmental and social effects of climate change separately.

Tree-of-Thought Prompting — I need to add real-time notifications to my app. Explore three different approaches — WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and polling — and for each one, explain the trade-offs in terms of complexity, scalability, and browser support. Then recommend which one fits a small team with a Node backend.

Tree-of-Thought Prompting — Instead of the AI just picking one and defending it (which is what zero-shot would do), this prompt makes the comparison explicit instead of letting the AI jump straight to one recommendation.

Tree-of-Thought Prompting — Another real use: Architecture decisions. "We need to store user sessions. Compare Redis, database sessions, and JWT tokens. For each: list pros, cons, and failure modes. Then recommend one for a team of two building an MVP."

Tree-of-Thought Prompting — When to use it: Any decision with multiple valid options where you need the AI to compare, not just pick. Tech stack choices, architecture decisions, debugging when you're not sure which subsystem is the problem.
Role-Playing Prompts — "You are a tech recruiter. What's weak about this resume?"
List every step that happens from when a user clicks "Login" to when they land on the dashboard — including token generation, cookie handling, and redirect logic.
What it is: Named after the Socratic method — you ask a question, then ask the AI to explain its own answer deeper, then deeper again. Recursive questioning until you actually understand.
Maieutic Prompting — "Explain why the sky is blue. Then explain why blue light scatters more."
Maieutic Prompting — Now explain why the dependency array matters for useMemo specifically.

The "list what you know first" step acts as a self-fact-check. What it is: Named after the Socratic method — you ask a question, then ask the AI to explain its own answer deeper, then deeper again. Recursive questioning until you actually understand. "Explain why the sky is blue. Then explain why blue light scatters more." Why is my React component re-rendering on every state change even though I'm using useMemo? Now explain why the dependency array matters for useMemo specifically. Now explain what "referential equality" means in the context of JavaScript objects and why it breaks memoization. Each follow-up forces the AI to go one layer deeper. By the third question, you've gone from "it's re-rendering" to understanding how JavaScript's object comparison model fundamentally interacts with React's reconciliation algorithm. When to use it: Learning new concepts. When the first answer makes sense but you can feel there's something underneath you don't fully get. It's the "but why?" technique. What it is: You tell the AI to break a big problem into subproblems first, then solve each one in order. Decompose, then execute. "List the subproblems to solve 3x + 5 = 20, then solve each." I need to add Google OAuth to my Next.js app. Break this down into every subproblem I need to solve, in order. Then walk me through each one with code. Then the AI solves each one sequentially, and each step builds on the last. This is basically how I survived every hackathon deadline — breaking "build a working demo in 24 hours" into an actual ordered sequence instead of staring at the whole scope and panicking. When to use it: Implementing features you've never built before. Instead of asking "how do I add auth" (which gets you a vague overview), you force the AI to give you a buildable sequence. What it is: You explicitly tell the AI what format you want the output in. Bullet points, table, JSON, markdown, CSV — specify it and the AI follows. Compare these three state management libraries for React. Output as a markdown table with columns: Library, Bundle Size, Learning Curve, Best For, and Drawback. Convert this error log into a JSON array where each object has timestamp, level, message, and source fields. This is one of the most underrated techniques. Most devs don't specify format and then spend 5 minutes reformatting the AI's response. Just tell it upfront. When to use it: Literally every time you want the output in a specific shape. Tables, JSON, code blocks, bullet points, numbered steps. If you're going to reformat the output anyway, you're wasting time. What it is: Building context across multiple messages in a conversation. Each prompt builds on the last response. This is how you turn AI from a search engine into a collaborator. Turn 1: "Summarize this article." Turn 2: "Now rewrite it for a 10-year-old." Turn 3: "Add three quiz questions." Turn 1: "Here's my Express app's folder structure. [paste tree output]. Explain the architecture."

"Outside your bubble" is hard when your bubble covers the whole site. I added discoveryMaxOverlap: Discover may share one followed tag, and strictly-outside posts still come first.

Since this is my introduction to fine-tuning, I wanted to pick something relatively simple, but also useful. Ideally, something that could save me or my fellow developers some money on AI API calls. It should be fast, work with an open-weight model, and actually make sense as a side hustle.
The idea is simple. Imagine you're using an expensive AI model for every request, even trivial ones like extracting a value from JSON or formatting some text.
Do you really need an expensive reasoning model for that? Probably not.

But your AI application doesn't necessarily know how complex an incoming prompt is, so it might send everything to the same model. That's where Complexity Scorer comes in. Before sending a prompt to an AI model, your application calls Complexity Scorer, a lightweight endpoint backed by a fine-tuned open-weight model. It estimates the prompt's complexity and returns a score between 0.00 and 1.00.
Your application can then use that score to decide which AI model should handle the actual request.

That's it. Of course, it's not limited to API endpoints. You could use it in AI agents, coding tools or any application that needs to choose between different models. And because it's based on an open-weight model, you could even run it locally using something like Ollama, once the fine-tuned model is exported into a compatible format.
The potential customers? Developers and teams building AI-powered applications who want to reduce their API costs without blindly routing everything to cheaper models.

Probably not. But your AI application doesn't necessarily know how complex an incoming prompt is, so it might send everything to the same model. That's where Complexity Scorer comes in. Before sending a prompt to an AI model, your application calls Complexity Scorer, a lightweight endpoint backed by a fine-tuned open-weight model. It estimates the prompt's complexity and returns a score between 0.00 and 1.00. Your application can then use that score to decide which AI model should handle the actual request. Complex problem? Send it to something more capable. That's it. Of course, it's not limited to API endpoints. You could use it in AI agents, coding tools or any application that needs to choose between different models. And because it's based on an open-weight model, you could even run it locally using something like Ollama, once the fine-tuned model is exported into a compatible format. The potential customers? Developers and teams building AI-powered applications who want to reduce their API costs without blindly routing everything to cheaper models. And how would I actually make money from this? Well, the model itself would remain free for anyone to download and use. I'd charge only for the convenience of using my hosted API, probably with a small free tier and monthly subscriptions that include a certain number of requests. Of course, the pricing would have to be low enough that developers actually save money by using Complexity Scorer. Otherwise, what's the point? Complexity Scorer estimates how much reasoning a prompt needs. Your application can use that estimate to choose which AI model should answer it, such as a cheaper model for a simple task or a more capable model for a difficult one. Send a prompt to POST /api/complexity and receive a score between 0.00 and 1.00. This endpoint evaluates the prompt; it does not answer it. Scores between these reference points are allowed. They are estimates, not guarantees that a particular model can solve the task. It scores the reasoning and understanding needed, rather than just the prompt's length: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science. Okay, let's start with the model training process, because this was probably the most interesting part of the whole project. To use Tinker, I first needed to set up a Python environment. I'm mostly a .NET developer, and I only use Python on rare occasions, so I had to install Python, the Tinker packages, and authenticate with Tinker. Fortunately, with a little help from ChatGPT, it was pretty straightforward. I ran into some trouble with Microsoft C++ Build Tools along the way, but nothing too dramatic. With the environment ready, I moved on to what might be the most important decision of the project: choosing the model to fine-tune. The open-weight model is the core of Complexity Scorer. My first selection criterion was simple: training cost on Tinker. After comparing the available models, I narrowed my options down to two of the cheapest candidates that seemed suitable for this task. GPT-OSS-20B is actually cheaper on paper, but there's a catch: it's a reasoning model that always generates chain-of-thought tokens before answering. That's not ideal for a classifier that's supposed to return a single number as quickly and cheaply as possible. Qwen3-8B, on the other hand, is a Hybrid model. It supports both thinking and non-thinking modes, which means we can disable reasoning for faster classification. And with a 32K context window, it should be more than enough for the prompts I want to classify. Now comes the interesting part: can I actually teach it to estimate prompt complexity? Okay, I didn't jump straight into fine-tuning. First, I started with a simple Python script (test_tinker.py) just to check whether I could actually call Tinker. Once that worked, I prepared a small evaluation dataset with 50 examples (eval.jsonl) and a baseline.py script to evaluate the selected model against it. My first evaluation was against the original Qwen3-8B, without any fine-tuning. The result? 50% accuracy. Not bad for a starting point. Next, I prepared 50 training examples (different from the evaluation dataset), saved them in train.jsonl, and ran my train.py script. After fine-tuning finished, I evaluated the model again using the same 50 evaluation examples. That was a little shocking, but also pretty exciting. Just 50 training examples and such a big improvement? Naturally, I thought that more training data would give me even better results. So I prepared another dataset with 500 training examples and trained the model again. I tried experimenting a little with the hyperparameters, but the accuracy stayed around 74%. And since I'm definitely not an ML engineer, I decided to stop experimenting with smoke tests and move on to the full fine-tuning run. At this point, I had everything prepared. The scripts worked, the evaluation dataset was ready, and I knew the model could learn the task. I chose 2,500 training examples as a balance between dataset diversity, generation effort, and training cost. With five complexity levels, that meant 500 examples per class, which sounded like a reasonable starting point. So I prepared a prompt and gave it to GPT-6.1 Sol with high thinking effort. I asked Sol to generate 2,500 training examples for my LLM. It started working, and I left it alone. Previously, generating 500 examples had taken around 30 minutes, so I expected this to take a while. But after approximately 47 minutes, things started looking suspicious. Still, I thought, well, 2,500 examples is a lot of data. Maybe it just needs more time. Meanwhile, I was browsing the web and randomly opened the billing tab on Tinker. I immediately stopped Sol and checked what it was actually doing. Instead of just generating training examples, it had started running model training in the background. synthesized_points: Ask almost any developer how object-oriented programming works, and they will describe the same textbook picture: an object bundles data and methods together into a single unit.
In Ruby, you hear this idea reinforced constantly under the slogan: "Everything is an object."

You create a string, call .upcase on it, and it feels completely natural to assume that the string object owns that method. You create a user object, call .save, and assume .save lives inside your user.

If you inspect an instance down at the C source code level in CRuby (MRI), you discover something surprising: an object stores its instance variables, a set of internal flags, and a pointer to another structure. It does not contain a single line of method code, nor does it contain a method table.
To truly master Ruby, you have to look beneath the syntactic sugar and understand the mechanics of Ruby's object model: method tables, the hidden eigenclass, and the ancestry ladder.
An array of instance variables — @name set to "Alice", and @email set to "alice@example.com".
The Mystery of Singleton Methods — We already know that objects cannot hold methods. So :shout cannot live inside str1.
"Class Methods" Do Not Exist — Once you understand eigenclasses, one of the biggest myths in Ruby evaporates: there is no such thing as a "class method".

"Class Methods" Do Not Exist — In languages like Java or C++, a static method is a distinct language construct. But in Ruby, Post is not a special entity. Post is simply an object. It is an instance of the class Class.

"Class Methods" Do Not Exist — Because Post is an object, writing def Post.recent or def self.recent is doing the exact same thing as writing def str1.shout: it is defining a singleton method on an object.
"Class Methods" Do Not Exist — The :recent method does not live in Post, and it does not live in Class. It lives in Post's own private eigenclass (#<Class:Post>).

"Class Methods" Do Not Exist — In Ruby, there are only instance methods. What we call "class methods" are merely instance methods living on the singleton class of a class object. The entire language operates on one single, unified rule.
Prepended Modules on the Eigenclass — Any module added with prepend sits in front of the eigenclass.
Prepended Modules on the Class — If a module was prepended to the class, its methods override the class's own methods.
Included Modules on the Class — If a module was included in the class, it is inserted directly above the class in the hierarchy.
Object, Kernel, and BasicObject — The root ancestors shared by virtually all Ruby objects.
What Happens When Nothing Matches? — If Ruby climbs all the way to BasicObject without finding a matching method, it does not immediately raise an error.
What Happens When Nothing Matches? — Instead, Ruby walks back down to the starting receiver and starts the entire search again from step one, this time searching for a method named method_missing.

What Happens When Nothing Matches? — Because Kernel provides a default implementation of method_missing that raises NoMethodError, your program only crashes if no intermediate module or class intercepts it.
What Happens When Nothing Matches? — This two-pass search is what powers Ruby's famous metaprogramming libraries, from ActiveRecord dynamic finders to OpenStruct.
How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers — In CRuby, the answer is no, thanks to an internal optimization called Tagged Pointers (Immediate Values).

How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers — On a 64-bit operating system, memory addresses are aligned to 8-byte boundaries. That means the lowest 3 bits of any valid heap pointer are always 000.

How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers — When the Ruby virtual machine sees a value with the lowest bit set to 1, it knows: "This is not a heap pointer. This is the raw integer itself."

How "Everything Is an Object" Runs Fast: Tagged Pointers — When you call 42.even?, Ruby does not inspect a heap block. It detects the tagged pointer, looks up the method in the Integer class method table, and executes the code without a single byte of memory allocation or garbage collection overhead.

In Ruby, you hear this idea reinforced constantly under the slogan: "Everything is an object."

You create a string, call .upcase on it, and it feels completely natural to assume that the string object owns that method. You create a user object, call .save, and assume .save lives inside your user.

If you inspect an instance down at the C source code level in CRuby (MRI), you discover something surprising: an object stores its instance variables, a set of internal flags, and a pointer to another structure. It does not contain a single line of method code, nor does it contain a method table.
Where do methods actually live? How does Ruby know what to execute when you type user.greet? And what actually happens when you define a method on a single specific object?
To truly master Ruby, you have to look beneath the syntactic sugar and understand the mechanics of Ruby's object model: method tables, the hidden eigenclass, and the ancestry ladder.
When Ruby evaluates User.new, the virtual machine allocates a heap structure called an RObject.
Notice what is missing from user: the greet method is nowhere to be found.
Methods in Ruby live exclusively inside classes (represented internally as RClass).
The User class contains a hash table called m_tbl (the method table). When you define def greet, Ruby writes an entry into User's method table mapping the symbol :greet to its compiled bytecode body.

This separation is what makes Ruby memory-efficient. You can instantiate one hundred thousand User objects, and all one hundred thousand share the exact same method table inside User. The instances only hold their personal instance variables.
Now consider this famous Ruby feature: you can add a method to just one individual object without affecting any other instance of that class.
If objects cannot hold methods, and the class cannot hold this method, where on earth does shout live?
Ruby solves this by doing something brilliant: it quietly invents an invisible class on the fly.
The moment you define a method on str1, Ruby creates an anonymous, hidden class called an eigenclass (officially referred to as a singleton class).
When you call str1.shout, Ruby follows the klass pointer into #<Class:str1>, finds :shout, and runs it.
When you call str1.upcase, Ruby looks in #<Class:str1>, does not find :upcase, follows the superclass pointer up to String, finds :upcase, and runs it.
To regular code, the singleton class is almost completely transparent. You do not see it in str1.class (which still reports String). But you can prove it exists with Ruby's reflection methods:
Once you understand eigenclasses, one of the biggest myths in Ruby evaporates: there is no such thing as a "class method".
Tutorials often say: "This defines a class method on Post."
In languages like Java or C++, a static method is a distinct language construct. But in Ruby, Post is not a special entity. Post is simply an object. It is an instance of the class Class.
Because Post is an object, writing def Post.recent or def self.recent is doing the exact same thing as writing def str1.shout: it is defining a singleton method on an object.
The :recent method does not live in Post, and it does not live in Class. It lives in Post's own private eigenclass (#<Class:Post>).

In Ruby, there are only instance methods. What we call "class methods" are merely instance methods living on the singleton class of a class object. The entire language operates on one single, unified rule.
When you type receiver.message, what is the exact order Ruby follows to find the code?
Ruby does not search haphazardly. It walks an exact, deterministic ladder called the ancestors chain. The first match it encounters executes immediately.
If Ruby climbs all the way to BasicObject without finding a matching method, it does not immediately raise an error.
Instead, Ruby walks back down to the starting receiver and starts the entire search again from step one, this time searching for a method named method_missing.
Because Kernel provides a default implementation of method_missing that raises NoMethodError, your program only crashes if no intermediate module or class intercepts it.
This two-pass search is what powers Ruby's famous metaprogramming libraries, from ActiveRecord dynamic finders to OpenStruct.
