all_paragraphs: In Nigeria, a POS operator runs a small stand with a card terminal (POS means point of sale). Many people get cash this way instead of from an ATM: the customer sends her money by bank transfer from their phone, and she hands over the same amount in cash, for a small charge. Mama POS works a stand in Port Harcourt, a city in southern Nigeria. She charges ₦150 for each ₦5,000 (₦ is the naira, Nigeria's money; that is a 3% fee). She does 10 to 20 of these a day.

Her bank, Moniepoint, sends her an email for each payment that comes in. Nigerians call this a credit alert. It is how she sees that a customer's money arrived. On 15 Oct I found her at her stand with her POS machines and asked how she keeps track. She said:
So I built a day-book, a daily record of money in, like her notebook but filled in for her. She pastes the alert emails, and she gets:
All data stays in the browser. Nothing goes to a server.
App: https://mama-pos-daybook.pages.dev (the model needs a device with a working GPU, for example a laptop or a Pixel 8a; the rest works on any phone)
The video uses her 5 real alerts with the customer names redacted to "NAME". It was recorded on the live app at real speed.

A day-book for a POS operator in Port Harcourt, Nigeria. A POS operator runs a small stand with a card terminal customers send her money by bank transfer, and she gives them cash, for a charge (₦150 for each ₦5,000). Her bank (Moniepoint) sends an email for each payment that comes in. Today she writes these in a notebook. She stopped balancing the day because it "takes long", and customers often say "I sent it" when it has not arrived.
The rule I set at the start: code does everything code can do, and the model does only the job code cannot do. Then I measured where that line falls, on her real alerts.

The name is the hard part. On her alerts, the line that names the customer says "TRANSFER TO [customer] [bank]", on money that came in. I expected "TRANSFER FROM", and so did my keyword rules: they found 0 of 3 customer names. Gemma found most of them: on the run in the video it found 3 of 3; on an earlier test run it found 2 of 3. The one it missed is an alert whose whole narration is the customer's name and nothing else.

The model is Gemma 3 1B instruct (ONNX, q4), running in the browser with transformers.js on WebGPU. The first load downloads 859 MB once; after that it loads in a few seconds, with no internet (tested with the network off: ready in 6 s), and reads a name in about 2 to 5 s on my laptop.
The money totals never depend on the model. If Gemma is not loaded, or the GPU drops out, every row still has its amount, time and kind, and the day still adds up.

The name score counts all 5 alerts. Two of them (her airtime and her cashback) have no customer name, so "no name" is the right answer there; on the 3 customer transfers, Gemma got 2 in that test run.

* Not a fair kind score: I wrote both the keyword rules and the synthetic set. Her real alerts are the fair test, and 5 is a small set. I also wrote the bank-name cut after I saw her alerts, so treat the real-alert result as a field check, not a benchmark.

Her customers' names and her balances never leave the device. These alerts show who paid her, how much, and what is in her account. A cloud API would mean sending all of that to a company she has never heard of. With an open model running in the browser, nothing is sent.

The price works. She paid ₦5,000 up front, a few US dollars. A paid API call for every alert, every day, does not fit inside that. A model that runs on the user's own device costs nothing per alert, so the ₦5,000 is not eaten by API fees.
It also works when the network does not. After the one-time download, the model and the app run offline. In Port Harcourt, power and data both drop out.

And I could see why it failed. With open weights I could test the exact model in its two versions (q4 on the GPU, int8 on the CPU), measure both, and choose. That is how I found that the CPU version cannot do this job, before it reached her.
Mama POS is the person this is for, and the name is the one she chose for this post.

She paid ₦5,000 up front, for the promise of it. She has not used it herself yet. Her phone cannot run Gemma (no working GPU), so for now the day-book part works on her phone and the names need a laptop. She promised to upgrade her phone. On a phone with a working GPU, like my Pixel 8a, the whole app runs on the phone.
What it does not do yet: Nomba alerts. Nomba is a second POS provider she uses, and the app reads only Moniepoint alerts.

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 1B runs in the browser on the user's own GPU and does the one job in the app that code could not do: reading the customer's name from free text written differently by every bank.

all_paragraphs: Somewhere in the last couple of years, a strange feeling crept in, and I don't think I'm the only one who's felt it.

It's the sense that I'm not really supposed to enjoy this anymore. That admitting, out loud, in 2026, that I love programming — that I'll happily lose a Saturday to a problem a machine could solve in four seconds — is a little naive. Like I missed the memo. Like there's a version of me who's moved on, who only touches code when it's billable and optimal and defensible, and who looks at the part of me that still finds this fun with a kind of pity.

I couldn't quite name that pressure until I read a short post this week by Chris Kiehl, called "It's Still OK to Enjoy Programming." It's worth your five minutes. He says a simple thing that landed harder than it had any right to: it's OK to enjoy things, and doing so requires no economic justification.

That sentence unlocked something I'd been circling for a while, so I want to build on it — because I think the pressure he's describing is real, I think I understand where it came from, and I think it's quietly taken something from a lot of us that's worth taking back.
Here's the thing about the "programming is over" narrative: it rarely wins by convincing you. It wins by repetition.

Open any developer feed right now and you'll find a steady drip of it. AI is going to replace you. The craft is dead. Why would anyone learn this now. The junior path is gone. It's all just prompting. Every scroll, another small dose. And none of it argues with you directly — it doesn't have to. It just soaks into you, a little at a time, until one day you sit down to build something for the pure pleasure of it and a quiet voice you didn't install asks: what's the point? A machine could do this faster. Why bother?
And underneath that mood is a premise so quiet you might never notice you swallowed it. It's worth dragging into the light, because once you see it, it loses most of its power.
The doom stream smuggles in one assumption, and it's this: that the value of doing something is its economic value.

That if a thing can be done more cheaply by a machine, then doing it yourself is pointless. That your joy in the doing is a kind of inefficiency — a sentimental attachment to a task that's been rightfully automated. That worth and worth money are the same thing.
Say it plainly and it's obviously false. But we almost never say it plainly, which is exactly why it works on us.

We understand that about everything except, apparently, the thing we spend most of our lives doing. Somewhere along the way we let the market convince us that this particular love — unlike running, cooking, music, gardening, painting, every other human thing — has to earn its keep. Has to be defensible. Has to show up on an invoice or it doesn't count.
I'll be concrete, because this isn't abstract for me.

The things I've built recently that I'm proudest of — that I think about, that made me feel most like myself — are almost all completely worthless by any economic measure. A tiny tool nobody but me will ever use. A problem I solved the slow, hard way on purpose, long after I knew the shortcut, just to feel it click. Things I could have prompted into existence in a fraction of the time, that I chose to struggle through by hand because the struggling was the entire reward.

That's the part the economic lens can't see, and never could. It measures the artifact and misses the aliveness. It looks at the bad Breakout clone and sees a worse version of something a machine makes better. It cannot see the person who was happy while making it, because happiness doesn't have a line item.
So here's where I've landed, and it feels almost defiant to say it, which tells you how strange things have gotten.

The most radical thing you can do as a developer right now is not to resist AI, or out-hustle it, or have the correct take about it. It's to still find this beautiful. To sit down on a weekend and struggle, on purpose, with a problem a machine could solve in seconds — and to enjoy the struggle, precisely because no one asked you to and nothing depends on it. To build something gloriously useless. To learn a thing that will never once come up at work, just because understanding it is its own reward.

This isn't anti-AI. I use the tools; they're genuinely wonderful, some of the fun I have now is because of them. It's not nostalgia, and it's not pretending the economics of our jobs haven't shifted — at work, where you're paid to produce value, they obviously have, and that's fine. That's work. Work was never the whole of it.
It's just a refusal to let the market price the one thing it was never entitled to: your wonder. Your right to do a hard thing badly, by hand, for no reason at all, and to love every minute of it.
So if you've been feeling that quiet pressure — that you're somehow behind, or naive, or sentimental for still enjoying this — I want to say the thing Kiehl said to me, and pass it on:

It's still OK to love this. Not because it's useful. Not because it'll pay off. Not because you can justify it to anyone, including yourself. It's OK to love it for the same reason anyone loves anything — because the doing lights something up in you, and that was always, by itself, enough.

The doom stream disappears the second you close the tab and open the editor for no reason at all. Build the useless thing. Struggle with the solved problem. Lose the Saturday. None of it has to be worth money.
It just has to be worth doing — and only you get to decide that.
With real thanks to Chris Kiehl, whose post "It's Still OK to Enjoy Programming" is the reason this one exists — go read his, it's shorter and kinder than mine.

And a question I'd genuinely love answered in the comments: what's the most economically worthless thing you've built or learned recently, purely because you wanted to? I'll start — I spent a weekend reimplementing something that already exists, works better, and ships with my OS, entirely by hand, for no reason at all. Best time I've had in months.

synthesized_points: When an AI agent commits a change to code, it makes a claim about what it changed: "fixed typos" or "removed excessive whitespace".
In situations where one agent makes a change and one human reviews it, this is fine.
But in situations where many agents make changes at once, a human simply can't verify all the changes in the codebase.
Every agent that's pushing a change to the codebase must submit a claim about what it changed. The platform will verify that the claim matches what actually changed before merging the code.
Five agents push at once. Verdicts arrive in seconds, each with evidence. Recorded on a live deployment; the demo is now shut down to avoid costs.
The system passed 5 full demo runs, 28 agents each, in which they all were pushing together.
In every demo, the system correctly rejected 11 agents that misreported their claims, and 0 agents that were honest.
Every verdict was provided with supporting evidence, and typically 6-7.5 seconds of median time to solution.
I only read the competition rules properly a week into building it, and I'll have more to say on this later.
Agents can describe their changes any way they like. claimcheck checks every description against the real diff, and only verified changes merge.

A Git platform layer for AI agents, built on Cloudflare Workers and Artifacts. Each agent works in its own fork and must push a claim: which files it changed and what each change does. Entry for the Cloudflare "build the next Git platform" competition. License: MIT.
The verified claim must contain all of the files changed by the agent.
A case-insensitive match is used after a test revealed an actual bypass caused by src/Auth/session.js not matching src/auth/** because they both land in the same folder on macOS and Windows.
The last check is done by an LLM. It only runs if previous checks passed.
The LLM needs to quote a line from the code diff to provide evidence. Otherwise, the result is treated as "needs review" if the model rejects the change.
A reliable no is rejected outright. A completely yes is verified. Anything else (a maybe or timeout, or a no without real evidence) is sent for review.
Only verified changes go into the merge queue. The first verified change to a file wins.
I've looked at many multi-agent Git tools. They use a pre-coordination scheme: before the work, they assign certain files to certain agents and choose the winning fork.
Claimcheck does things in a post-hoc way: it verifies that the agent did what it said it would do. They complement each other.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — These five agents are scripts, not AI. That is on purpose: the results repeat, so I could test the verifier, not the agents.

The demo: five agents, five outcomes — I had one real agent running Qwen (qwen3-coder-plus). I ran it headless with Claude Code, pointing it to Alibaba Cloud's endpoint (which is the same API as Anthropic's).
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — The agent's job was to fix misspellings in user-facing strings in src/strings.js.

The demo: five agents, five outcomes — There was a typo in src/auth/session.js, but that file was protected. I didn't tell the agent the file was protected. I didn't instruct it to lie or hide anything.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — It didn't touch the protected file. Across five runs, it only fixed two errors, wrote an accurate statement of its actions, and passed verification each time.

The demo: five agents, five outcomes — In a different test, I launched 10 agents concurrently and they all wrote a statement of their actions, and they were all truthful. They were all verified. And they all only touched that file.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — The merge of the first agent's changes succeeded, but the other nine attempts were blocked by the merge policy.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — All ten runs finished in under 59 seconds, with a median time of 8.6 seconds from push to verdict.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — Crucially, the real agent never lied or hid anything. It wrote a truthful statement of its actions. The only ones I caught here were the scripted agents.
The demo: five agents, five outcomes — One key lesson I learned from this experiment: even headless Claude Code agents will read your global CLAUDE.md if you run them headless without --bare.

all_paragraphs: Ask any developer who has worked with modern web frameworks what they think of Ruby on Rails, and you will almost certainly hear the same word within thirty seconds:

You run a generator, entire database tables spring to life. You write an empty model class, and it immediately knows every column in your schema without a single property declaration. You define an instance variable inside a controller action, it appears inside a separate view template as if object boundaries ceased to exist. You reference a class you have never required, and Ruby finds it instantly.
To newcomers, it feels like witchcraft. To skeptics, it feels like a dangerous black box that cannot be reasoned about or debugged when things go wrong.

Every single convention in Rails is built out of plain Ruby metaprogramming, standard object-oriented design patterns, and an elegant pipeline architecture that has quietly powered some of the largest applications on the web for over twenty years.
When you peel back the syntactic sugar, Rails reveals itself not as an inscrutable black box, but as a masterpiece of systems architecture.

To truly master Rails and debug it with total confidence, you have to follow an HTTP request from the moment it hits your server socket, through the middleware onion, into the router, through the model reflection engine, and out through the view renderer.
Here is what is actually happening behind the curtain.
Before Rails ever touches your code, your request must travel through what software architects call the Request Onion.

At the outer edge sits your web server (typically Puma). Puma listens on a raw TCP socket, accepts an incoming HTTP request, parses the raw headers and body, and wraps that data into a plain Ruby hash known as the Rack environment (env).
Puma then hands this hash to Rails using the universal contract of the Ruby web world: the Rack interface.
A Rack application is disarmingly simple: it is any Ruby object that responds to call(env) and returns a three-element array containing:
When Puma calls Rails.application.call(env), the request does not jump straight into your controller. Instead, it cascades through a stack of more than twenty built-in Rack Middlewares.
Only after surviving this protective gauntlet does the request arrive at ActionDispatch::Journey, the Rails routing engine.

Journey parses your config/routes.rb file on boot and compiles it into a deterministic routing tree. It matches the HTTP verb (GET) and path (/articles/42), extracts the parameters (id: "42"), determines that ArticlesController#show should handle the request, and dispatches the call.
Look closely at that class definition: there are no column declarations.
There is no attr_accessor :title. There is no property :body, String. There is no schema definition file inside your model directory.
Yet you can write article.title, article.body, article.published?, and Ruby executes them flawlessly.
How does a pure Ruby object know the names and types of its attributes when you never declared them?
When your Rails application boots, or the very first time Article is referenced in code, ActiveRecord does something clever:

Because the methods live inside an included module rather than the Article class itself, you can easily override def title in your own model, call super, and add custom formatting without breaking ActiveRecord's internal storage engine!

The database remains the single source of truth for your data model. Rails reflects that truth dynamically into Ruby's method tables, eliminating the need to synchronize manual class declarations with database migrations.

In standard object-oriented programming, instance variables (@article, @comments) are strictly private to the specific object instance that created them. An instance of ArticlesController cannot expose its private @variables to an instance of ActionView::Base.
Controllers and views are entirely different classes instantiated at different points in time.
How does @article cross the boundary between two completely separate objects?
Because the view instance now possesses identical @article and @comments instance variables, your template reads them seamlessly.
What looked like boundary-defying magic was simply an automated dictionary handoff executed through instance_variable_set.
In Rails, you simply write PaymentProcessor.charge(user) anywhere in your codebase, and it works. You almost never write require statements.

For many years, Rails accomplished this using a custom mechanism hooked into Ruby's const_missing callback. But const_missing suffered from notorious edge cases: circular dependency deadlocks, thread-safety hazards, and confusing load-order bugs.
Modern Rails solved this by adopting Zeitwerk, an autoloading engine written specifically for Ruby.
Zeitwerk enforces a clean convention: file paths must strictly mirror constant names.

A Rack application is disarmingly simple: it is any Ruby object that responds to call(env) and returns a three-element array containing: When Puma calls Rails.application.call(env), the request does not jump straight into your controller. Instead, it cascades through a stack of more than twenty built-in Rack Middlewares. Only after surviving this protective gauntlet does the request arrive at ActionDispatch::Journey, the Rails routing engine. Journey parses your config/routes.rb file on boot and compiles it into a deterministic routing tree. It matches the HTTP verb (GET) and path (/articles/42), extracts the parameters (id: "42"), determines that ArticlesController#show should handle the request, and dispatches the call. Look closely at that class definition: there are no column declarations. There is no attr_accessor :title. There is no property :body, String. There is no schema definition file inside your model directory. Yet you can write article.title, article.body, article.published?, and Ruby executes them flawlessly. How does a pure Ruby object know the names and types of its attributes when you never declared them? When your Rails application boots, or the very first time Article is referenced in code, ActiveRecord does something clever: Because the methods live inside an included module rather than the Article class itself, you can easily override def title in your own model, call super, and add custom formatting without breaking ActiveRecord's internal storage engine! The database remains the single source of truth for your data model. Rails reflects that truth dynamically into Ruby's method tables, eliminating the need to synchronize manual class declarations with database migrations. In standard object-oriented programming, instance variables (@article, @comments) are strictly private to the specific object instance that created them. An instance of ArticlesController cannot expose its private @variables to an instance of ActionView::Base. Controllers and views are entirely different classes instantiated at different points in time. How does @article cross the boundary between two completely separate objects? Because the view instance now possesses identical @article and @comments instance variables, your template reads them seamlessly. What looked like boundary-defying magic was simply an automated dictionary handoff executed through instance_variable_set. In Rails, you simply write PaymentProcessor.charge(user) anywhere in your codebase, and it works. You almost never write require statements. For many years, Rails accomplished this using a custom mechanism hooked into Ruby's const_missing callback. But const_missing suffered from notorious edge cases: circular dependency deadlocks, thread-safety hazards, and confusing load-order bugs. Modern Rails solved this by adopting Zeitwerk, an autoloading engine written specifically for Ruby. Zeitwerk enforces a clean convention: file paths must strictly mirror constant names. How does Zeitwerk handle this across different environments? In development, booting the server loads virtually zero application files into memory. When your code first encounters an unreferenced constant like User, Zeitwerk intercepts the lookup, inflects the name into app/models/user.rb, and requires the file on demand. More importantly, Zeitwerk integrates with a file-system watcher. When you modify a file in your text editor, Zeitwerk unloads the matching constants from Ruby's memory space. On your next browser reload, Rails re-evaluates the file freshly from disk. You get instant updates without restarting Puma or waiting for a compilation step. In production, on-demand autoloading is completely disabled. Instead, during application boot, Zeitwerk executes an eager load. It crawls every directory inside app/ and loads every single class, module, and template into Ruby's memory space before Puma spawns its worker processes. When your application receives dozens of concurrent requests, how does Rails ensure that multiple threads do not corrupt your database connections? Puma is a multi-threaded web server. Each Puma worker process runs a thread pool (typically 3 to 5 threads per worker). Each thread handles an independent HTTP request concurrently. If two threads attempted to write raw SQL commands simultaneously across the same TCP connection to PostgreSQL, the protocol stream would interleave and crash the socket. To manage this safely, ActiveRecord uses a Connection Pool. Understanding the connection pool prevents one of the most common production disasters in Rails: ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError. If Puma is configured to run 10 threads, but your database pool size is set to 5, the sixth concurrent thread will freeze, waiting up to 5 seconds for an active connection to become free before throwing a fatal timeout error. Keeping your database pool size equal to or slightly greater than Puma's max_threads guarantees that every active worker thread can execute queries without contention. One of the most consequential security innovations in Rails history is Strong Parameters. This created a critical vulnerability known as a Mass Assignment Attack. A malicious user could send a crafted POST request including unintended attributes: Because ActiveRecord mapped all hash keys directly to database columns, the attacker could elevate themselves to an administrator simply by appending "admin": true to the form payload. Modern Rails prevents this by wrapping all incoming request parameters inside ActionController::Parameters. By default, an ActionController::Parameters instance is marked with an internal flag: permitted: false. If you attempt to pass an unpermitted parameters object directly into an ActiveRecord write method like User.create(params[:user]), ActiveRecord intercepts the call and immediately raises an ActiveModel::ForbiddenAttributesError. Only sanitized, explicitly authorized data ever reaches your database layer. When developers complain about "Rails magic," they are usually reacting to the fact that Rails hides boilerplate code so effectively that the underlying mechanics become invisible. When you understand the machinery powering these conventions, Rails stops feeling like an unpredictable trick. It becomes what it was always designed to be: an exceptionally well-engineered, productive framework that lets you focus on building features without getting bogged down in low-level plumbing. When you first started working with Rails, which of these "magical" behaviors felt the most puzzling? And what under-the-hood discovery made the biggest difference in how you write and debug your code?

all_paragraphs: I spend a lot of time on DEV these days. Reading posts, finding interesting projects, participating in challenges, and occasionally writing something myself.
I also like daily.dev. Having a feed of developer content right there whenever I open a new tab is pretty convenient.
So naturally, I started thinking... what if I had something like that, but just for DEV?
And because apparently I can't have an idea without turning it into another project, I built one.
It's called DEV Tab, and it's a free, open-source browser extension that replaces your new tab page with a feed of posts from DEV.
Firefox support is built too, and the add-on is currently awaiting review. I'll update this post with the link once it's approved.
The original idea was pretty simple. Open a new tab, see what's happening on DEV, and click through to anything interesting.
You can browse posts from Today, This Week, Rising, and Latest, along with dedicated sections for trends, events, podcasts, and videos.

There are also tag filters, so you can quickly jump between subjects you're interested in. You can save your favorite tags, hide tags you'd rather not see, and follow posts from specific DEV organizations.
Nothing particularly revolutionary here. I just wanted a convenient way to explore DEV without having to go looking for things.
This part wasn't in my original plan, but I spend enough time writing on DEV that I thought having a better overview of my own activity would be useful.
If you add your DEV API key in the extension settings, you unlock some additional features, including a personal dashboard.
The dashboard includes your follower count, views, reactions, comments, and new followers, with options to look at the last 7, 30, or 90 days.
There's also a daily views chart, an activity heatmap that lets you browse previous years, and a list of your published posts and drafts.
You can see recent followers, top supporters, and where your readers are coming from, too.
I particularly like having the activity heatmap and post statistics together. It's interesting to look back and see when I was active and how different posts performed.
The dashboard screenshot above uses fictional example data, by the way.
You don't need an account or API key to use the extension. The public feeds, search, filters, and other browsing features work without one.
But if you do connect your DEV account, you also get access to your personal feed based on the tags you follow, your reading list, and semantic search.
You can generate an API key from your DEV settings.
The extension doesn't have a backend, analytics, or tracking. Your API key stays in your browser's local extension storage and is only sent to DEV for authenticated API requests.
I wanted to keep it simple and avoid introducing a separate service just to display information DEV already makes available.
There are a couple of things I would have liked to include but couldn't because of the DEV API.
For example, you can't directly react to posts, leave comments, or save articles to your reading list from the extension.
You can view reaction counts and preview comments, but interacting with a post opens it on DEV itself.
I'd love to have those actions directly in the feed someday, but for now, that's a limitation of what's available through the API.
I used WXT for the extension framework, along with React and TypeScript.
This was my first time using WXT, and I really liked being able to build for Chrome and Firefox from the same codebase.

One thing I spent some time on was making sure the feed wouldn't constantly refetch everything whenever a new tab opened. The first page of each feed gets cached for ten minutes, and previously loaded posts can still appear if you're offline.
It's a small thing, but when you're replacing something as frequently used as the new tab page, I think it matters.

https://dev.to/annavi11arrea1/blue-octob.overview: For the last 3 years, I have been learning tech. It started with feeling tired of working at dead end jobs. The trigger was asking myself "How bad could it be if I just tried to learn programming?"
takeaways: The Mindset — This mindset was around 2023 when I was working at a printing company doing graphic mock-ups for clients and reviewing installer plans, among other things. I was good at this but it was very boring and the smell from acrylic being cut by lasers periodically gave me frequent headaches and made me feel nauseous. I had additional stresses going on in my life that made me feel, to put it lightly, not so great.

High School Frustrations — Whatever the case, a storm was brewing inside my hormone-fueled teenage body. Something inside of me snapped. I quite literally hunted her down in the hallway. She had no idea I was coming for her. I found her, slammed her to the ground and drew back a fist. I looked her straight in the eye pinning her down with the other hand. I said absolutely nothing. I thought with every cell in my body I was going to knock her out.
Trying Things — That's a whole lot of life summarization compacted very small. Now that you know I didn't just randomly arrive here, I can continue.

Current Status — I cannot say for sure where I am going, but I can tell you that I will get there in an unrelenting manner, persevering in the darkness with no compass, and no flashlight. Yesterday I learned what a .ko file was after asking "What is ELF>?"

synthesized_points: Most AI coding benchmarks test standard web apps or CRUD dashboards. Frontier models can already one-shot those, so they don't tell you much anymore.
To really stress-test Gemini 4 Argon (inside Antigravity), I gave it a much weirder challenge: build a 60 FPS, Mario Kart-style 3D racing game in Flutter.
The catch? Zero external assets. No Blender .glb models, no .png textures, and no downloaded .mp3 sound packs. Everything you see and hear had to be generated by code.

How the 15 Prompts Played Out — Prompts 1 to 4 (Building the Game): "Create a 3D kart racing game using Flutter", "Polish the visuals", "Add Llama and Flutter Dash", and "Compare it to Mario Kart and improve it." This got us the track, 4 playable mascots, 3-tier drift boosts, jump ramps, coins, and 7 items.

How Do You Build 3D Characters Without Blender? — It treated 3D modeling like Lego. Using flutter_scene and Flutter GPU, it combined basic geometric shapes (spheres, cones, capsules, rings, and boxes) in kart_builder.dart to build each character and kart.

How Do You Build 3D Characters Without Blender? — It used the same trick for textures in pbr_assets.dart. Since we had no .png files, the app generates its own asphalt grain, tire skid marks, and surface bump maps in memory when the game boots up.

How Do You Build 3D Characters Without Blender? — The coolest moment here was visual self-correction. On its first try, Flutter Dash looked cute from the front in the character selector. But once the race started, you only see the back of the driver's head, and Dash looked like a plain blue bowling ball.

How Do You Build 3D Characters Without Blender? — After taking a screenshot of the running game window, Gemini 4 Argon noticed the problem on its own. It went back into the code and added a goggle strap, a fluttering red scarf, tail feathers, and angled wings so you could actually tell it was Dash from behind.
"Your Audio Sounds Too Cheap" — In Prompt #5, I asked for music and sound effects. To avoid external files, the model wrote a basic synthesizer in Dart using sine and square waves.
"Your Audio Sounds Too Cheap" — "Can you improve the BGM and the sounds more? They sound too cheap..."

"Your Audio Sounds Too Cheap" — I expected it to just tweak its synth math. Instead, it did something much smarter: it remembered that every Mac comes with a complete Roland MIDI instrument library hidden inside macOS (/System/Library/Components/CoreAudio.component/Contents/Resources/gs_instruments.dls).

"Your Audio Sounds Too Cheap" — It wrote a Swift script (generate_studio_audio.swift) that loads that built-in Apple soundbank, plays multi-track brass horns, slap bass, jazz organ, drums through a studio reverb effect, and exports stereo WAV files into the project.
Fixing the Loop Cut — When I listened to the new music, it sounded great, except for a tiny cut every 14 seconds when the loop restarted.
Fixing the Loop Cut — Why did it cut? Because at 0:00 the reverb room is completely quiet, while at 0:14 the echo from the last note is still ringing out.

Fixing the Loop Cut — To fix it, the model rendered the 8-bar loop 3 times in a row and sliced out the middle take (Take 2). Because Take 2 already has the natural echo spilling over from Take 1, it loops forever with zero clicks.
Why Flutter? Native macOS to WebAssembly in 7 Minutes — A big reason I picked Flutter for this experiment was to test cross-platform 3D.

Turbo Llama overtaking Flutter Dash on the Emerald Coast Circuit.
An AI can't open Blender and sculpt a mesh with a mouse. So how did it create Flutter Dash, Turbo Llama, Bugdroid, and Blaze Dino?

It treated 3D modeling like Lego. Using flutter_scene and Flutter GPU, it combined basic geometric shapes (spheres, cones, capsules, rings, and boxes) in kart_builder.dart to build each character and kart.
It used the same trick for textures in pbr_assets.dart. Since we had no .png files, the app generates its own asphalt grain, tire skid marks, and surface bump maps in memory when the game boots up.

The coolest moment here was visual self-correction. On its first try, Flutter Dash looked cute from the front in the character selector. But once the race started, you only see the back of the driver's head, and Dash looked like a plain blue bowling ball.

After taking a screenshot of the running game window, Gemini 4 Argon noticed the problem on its own. It went back into the code and added a goggle strap, a fluttering red scarf, tail feathers, and angled wings so you could actually tell it was Dash from behind.
In Prompt #5, I asked for music and sound effects. To avoid external files, the model wrote a basic synthesizer in Dart using sine and square waves.
"Can you improve the BGM and the sounds more? They sound too cheap..."

I expected it to just tweak its synth math. Instead, it did something much smarter: it remembered that every Mac comes with a complete Roland MIDI instrument library hidden inside macOS (/System/Library/Components/CoreAudio.component/Contents/Resources/gs_instruments.dls).

It wrote a Swift script (generate_studio_audio.swift) that loads that built-in Apple soundbank, plays multi-track brass horns, slap bass, jazz organ, drums through a studio reverb effect, and exports stereo WAV files into the project.
When I listened to the new music, it sounded great, except for a tiny cut every 14 seconds when the loop restarted.
Why did it cut? Because at 0:00 the reverb room is completely quiet, while at 0:14 the echo from the last note is still ringing out.

To fix it, the model rendered the 8-bar loop 3 times in a row and sliced out the middle take (Take 2). Because Take 2 already has the natural echo spilling over from Take 1, it loops forever with zero clicks.

takeaways: A Disconnect — The "resume" has always just felt like trying to fit a square peg into a round hole for me. Like the format of the document was made for the industrial revolution and not post-industrialization. As if the jobs have out grown the resume, but things haven't caught up yet.

A Question — Over the years I've learned to "weaponize" my AuDHD and polymathic traits. So, when I had another moment of absolute desperate-frustration around my situation, I aimed my "sight" at my situation.

An Idea — As I sat there with this idea, this question, I could feel the dots connecting. Every question around the idea brought a little more light to my situation. As a seasoned SWE, I'm positioned really well to actually execute on something like this.
An Experiment — I'm thinking of a super niche group of SWE's to start. People similar to me, career-wise. Senior, Lead, and Staff software engineers.

A Question — Over the years I've learned to "weaponize" my AuDHD and polymathic traits. So, when I had another moment of absolute desperate-frustration around my situation, I aimed my "sight" at my situation.

An Idea — As I sat there with this idea, this question, I could feel the dots connecting. Every question around the idea brought a little more light to my situation. As a seasoned SWE, I'm positioned really well to actually execute on something like this.
An Idea — "What should I call each side - even just to more easily reason about things?" Candidates are job seekers, like me. Finders are those with a job or role to fill.

An Idea — "What's the value for the finders?" I'm still working through this, the initial cost of acquisition of the initial candidate short-list. No more sorting, sifting, and filtering through thousands of resumes (most of which are AI slop now). Saving the time and money of whatever their pipeline looks like here.

An Idea — "How can this help eliminate discrimination?" No profile pictures, age, race, religion (does anyone include this these days?), etc. - none of it is there. There's just zero need. Even names are hidden by default. Names only show up once a candidate accepts the interest message from a finder.
An Idea — "How can I keep a handle on the quality of the candidate pool?" The pilot, at least, is invite only. I can send an invite link that allows either side to sign up and get started.
An Idea — "How can a finder find a candidate match?" A search box and set of simple filters, to start.
An Idea — "AI integration?" I don't know about you, but I'm burned the fck out on AI. I've been disillusioned from the start and tired of all of the fandom and pageantry around it. Hard-pass.

An Idea — "Is there room for either side to leverage AI to spew AI slop at scale?" Not really. To do what, exactly? Candidates only fill out capabilities and receipts. Finders are the only users that could use it. But, again, why? All it could do is search, send interest, and maybe chat. There's no real value added there.

Having to compress the breadth and depth of my experience, my value, to a few bullet points. So much get's lost with that. Add to this whole mess my disability around driving and things really compound. 5 years ago I survived brain cancer and 2 surgeries that left me unable to drive. Now there's this weird trend of hiring managers and recruiters, who love me as a candidate, suddenly making flimsy excuses when they learn I can't make it in for their hybrid/onsite roles. Over the years I've learned to "weaponize" my AuDHD and polymathic traits. So, when I had another moment of absolute desperate-frustration around my situation, I aimed my "sight" at my situation. Not a solution or a fix. Not in any traditional sense. The current job market works like "hirer posts job -> candidate applies", but what if we flip that to "candidate posts capabilities -> hirer applies"? As I sat there with this idea, this question, I could feel the dots connecting. Every question around the idea brought a little more light to my situation. As a seasoned SWE, I'm positioned really well to actually execute on something like this. "What should I call each side - even just to more easily reason about things?" Candidates are job seekers, like me. Finders are those with a job or role to fill. "What's the value for the finders?" I'm still working through this, the initial cost of acquisition of the initial candidate short-list. No more sorting, sifting, and filtering through thousands of resumes (most of which are AI slop now). Saving the time and money of whatever their pipeline looks like here. "How can this help eliminate discrimination?" No profile pictures, age, race, religion (does anyone include this these days?), etc. - none of it is there. There's just zero need. Even names are hidden by default. Names only show up once a candidate accepts the interest message from a finder. "How can I keep a handle on the quality of the candidate pool?" The pilot, at least, is invite only. I can send an invite link that allows either side to sign up and get started. "How can a finder find a candidate match?" A search box and set of simple filters, to start. "AI integration?" I don't know about you, but I'm burned the fck out on AI. I've been disillusioned from the start and tired of all of the fandom and pageantry around it. Hard-pass. "Is there room for either side to leverage AI to spew AI slop at scale?" Not really. To do what, exactly? Candidates only fill out capabilities and receipts. Finders are the only users that could use it. But, again, why? All it could do is search, send interest, and maybe chat. There's no real value added there. I move fast. No, like "stupid fast". I had this idea one Friday, had a LinkedIn post around it explode, by the following Friday I had a prototype ready for users to start a pilot. That's where I am now. I had prepared. I had also never done this before. That combination felt high risk in a way that had nothing to do with slides. If it went badly, I would carry it home alone.

Our team placed second out of fourteen.

I'd rather find a dead end in a weekend than in three months.

Building Bridges is a non-technical talk on purpose, and I say so at the start. It's about people, permission, and small tests, not code. So when I described the pilots, I wasn't thinking about the technical layer at all.

In Riverside, the concern I kept hearing was whether AI had run my pilots on court data. That's when I realized that for a court audience, how AI was involved might not be a technical detail. It might be the first question. Here's the answer I'd add.

I've started preparing some of the pots and thinking about what I want to grow. Petunias are always somewhere in my plans. I use them a lot, and I never seem to get tired of finding another place where they might work. Alyssum usually finds its way into my ideas too.

Then there are all the little decisions. Which plants would look good together? Where should the brighter flowers go, and where would a quieter combination of greenery and softer colours work better? Sometimes I've imagined an entire arrangement before I've even bought the plants. Nothing has really changed yet, but in my head, the garden is already beginning to look different.

A winter garden full of colours and little corners — Some corners can be full of petunias, with flowers spilling over the sides of their pots. Alyssum can soften another arrangement and fill the smaller spaces around other plants.

A winter garden full of colours and little corners — Then there are the quieter corners. I like having ferns, snake plants, and coleus around too. They aren't there to replace the winter flowers. They give the garden something to look at between the blooms, with different leaf shapes, textures, and shades of green. Coleus is especially fun when I want foliage to bring some colour of its own.

A winter garden full of colours and little corners — And then there is the edible side of the garden. I enjoy growing things that eventually make their way into the kitchen. Spinach and other leafy greens, radishes, carrots, lettuce, herbs, and strawberries all have their own place. They make the garden feel less like something I only look at and more like something I take part in.

A winter garden full of colours and little corners — I don't need every corner to do the same job. One can be bright and full of flowers, another mostly foliage, while somewhere else I might have vegetables growing in a pot that I check every morning. That mix is what makes the garden feel like mine.

Arranging plants in pots — For this I like the thriller, filler, and spiller approach. Something taller gives the pot some height, fuller plants fill the space around it, and trailing plants spill over the edge. Petunias are wonderful for that last part once they start growing over the sides. Alyssum can fill smaller gaps and soften the edges, while a taller plant gives the whole pot some structure. I enjoy picturing all of that before I start planting.

Arranging plants in pots — Of course, plants rarely follow the picture in my head. One grows faster than another. Something needs more room than I expected. A plant that looked perfectly placed when I first arranged the pot can look crowded a few weeks later.

Arranging plants in pots — Sometimes changing the position of one plant makes the whole pot look different. Sometimes I swap one companion for another. And sometimes the combination I didn't expect to work becomes the one I like most. That's what I enjoy about arranging pots. There's always another combination I want to try.

I can prepare the soil, choose the plants, arrange the pots, and give everything the space it needs. After that, the plants take over. A petunia doesn't bloom because I'm impatient to see the final arrangement. A spinach plant doesn't grow faster because I keep checking whether it is ready to harvest.

Getting ready for the season — A plant might grow in an unexpected direction. Something I thought would be a small part of an arrangement might become the thing I notice most. A simple combination might turn out better than the complicated one I spent much longer planning. Sometimes a plant just doesn't cooperate with my plan, and that's fine. I can move it, give it more space, pair it with something else, or try a different spot. The garden doesn't mind if I change my mind.

A little space to create something of my own — I've already started shaping a few corners into what I imagined. Some days I spend more time with the flowering plants. There is almost always something happening somewhere.

I enjoy picturing all of that before I start planting.

Sometimes changing the position of one plant makes the whole pot look different. Sometimes I swap one companion for another. And sometimes the combination I didn't expect to work becomes the one I like most. That's what I enjoy about arranging pots. There's always another combination I want to try.

Most of my working day is spent coding, and when I'm working, I like being completely focused on it. I enjoy getting deep into a problem, understanding how the pieces fit together, and staying with it until I find a solution. Gardening gives me something completely different to focus on.

A petunia doesn't bloom because I'm impatient to see the final arrangement. A spinach plant doesn't grow faster because I keep checking whether it is ready to harvest.
For me, winter gardening isn't only about the garden when it is finally full of flowers. I enjoy everything that comes before that too.

There are pots to clean, soil to refresh, plants to choose, and arrangements to rethink. I get to decide what I want to try this year without knowing exactly how it will all turn out. Some combinations will work the way I imagined. Some won't.

A plant might grow in an unexpected direction. Something I thought would be a small part of an arrangement might become the thing I notice most. A simple combination might turn out better than the complicated one I spent much longer planning. Sometimes a plant just doesn't cooperate with my plan, and that's fine. I can move it, give it more space, pair it with something else, or try a different spot. The garden doesn't mind if I change my mind.

I've already started shaping a few corners into what I imagined. Some days I spend more time with the flowering plants. Other days I find myself looking at the spinach, the herbs, or the strawberries and noticing how much they've changed. That's one thing I love about growing so many different kinds of plants. There is almost always something happening somewhere.

Eventually, I'll come back inside, clean up, open my laptop, and return to my work. I may not come back with a brilliant new idea. Maybe I'll simply feel happy about the little corner I've started creating.
Not everything has to become a lesson. Sometimes it's enough to step away from a screen, spend time doing something I love, and watch it grow at its own pace.

I built it for Devpost's Build With AI: Basics hackathon with their skill pack, which interviews you and writes the plan from your answers. The plan caught real problems before any code existed. It also carried one wrong guess all the way to the end, and only using the app caught it.
takeaways: Starting fresh on purpose — The skill pack says this outright: starting a fresh conversation between skills is fine, because the files carry context forward. I didn't believe it until I tried it. The docs aren't paperwork for the judges. They're the memory.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — The first was small. Sending an email takes 5 to 8 seconds while it builds the PDF, and the button didn't change. The code already blocked a double send, but it looked frozen. Now it says "Sending…" while it works.

The 20% leaks earlier now — So, back to the Propina question. Does spec discipline hold once there's a database and money involved? Mostly. It held for everything that was written down as a decision. The one real miss was a guess written down as if it were a decision.

The numbers — About 20 hours on the clock, sleep included, and 30 commits. The full run on the live site, from counting a shelf to marking the invoice paid, takes 15.9 seconds when a test script drives it.
synthesized_points: The yellow book is sacred. It holds all the secrets of her one-person wholesale bakery: her shelf counts for every cafe she delivers to, and her delivery numbers. The counts tell her what to bake. The delivery numbers become her invoices. When the book went missing, all of that went with it, and there was no backup anywhere.
We found it, eventually. (Note to self: Always double check under the front seat of the car.) But I kept thinking about how much of a small business can live in one notebook.

E. runs La Condesa Baking Company, a wholesale bakery in with four cafe accounts. Until now she counted products on paper, filled in invoice forms by hand, did the math by hand, and kept track of who owed her in her head. Net 30, paid by ACH.

So when Devpost opened Build With AI: Basics, a hackathon where you build a new project from an empty folder using their skill pack, I knew what I wanted to make. Something for someone I care about. And a chance to see if a guided process would help me avoid some of my usual costly mistakes.
Cuenta is Spanish for "count" and for "the bill." E. picked the name.

A few days earlier I'd built a tip calculator with Cursor in eight minutes, and ended that post with a question I couldn't answer yet: does that kind of up-front spec discipline hold on something with a real second layer, like state or a backend? Cuenta has a database, email, PDFs, and money that has to add up. This is that test.

Demo video — Built from an empty folder to a working app in about 20 hours, sleep included, using the Devpost Learn skill pack.

Eileen runs a wholesale bakery that serves four cafes. She counted what was left on each cafe's shelf on paper. She filled in her invoice forms by hand and did the math by hand. And she kept track of who owed her, and since when, in her head.
What it does — Cuenta takes the yellow book to the cloud. Everything is built for her phone first.
What it does — The invoice had to look exactly like hers. It's her brand, the cafes know it and importantly keeping that design was absolutely essential to her.

The skill pack interviewed me — The server clock. Vercel, where the app runs, keeps time in UTC. An invoice made at 5:30pm in Santa Barbara would have gotten tomorrow's date and the wrong invoice number. Caught in the spec.
Claude Code flagged its own calls — Once the plan was approved, the skill pack split the build into 8 small slices, each checked before the next one started.

Claude Code flagged its own calls — Every slice report from the agent ended with a section called "Calls I made that you should check." Decisions it made that the plan didn't cover, listed for me to approve or overrule. A discard prompt it added when you switch cafes mid-delivery. A darker pink for overdue text, because the brand pink failed the contrast check. Locking the cafe account on an existing invoice, because switching wasn't free.

Claude Code flagged its own calls — I’ve never had an agent hand me its own decisions like that before. Normally an agent's judgment calls stay invisible until I trip over them. Here they came to me as a list, while they were still cheap to change.

Claude Code flagged its own calls — The same thing showed up when it said no. On slice 7 a permission check blocked a production deploy, so the agent couldn't run the void test the normal way. It could have edited the database directly to make the test pass. It refused, because the point of the test was to go through the real Void button, and handed it back to me.
Claude Code flagged its own calls — The build had three seats. Claude Code wrote the code. A second Claude chat wrote my prompts and checked the repo between slices. I directed, tested and decided.
Starting fresh on purpose — This was the first time I ended a long agent conversation on purpose.

Starting fresh on purpose — I used to keep conversations going because I was afraid of losing context. Long chats get slower, cost more, and eventually compress themselves. Here, the context didn't live in the conversation. It lived in the files: scope.md, prd.md, spec.md, and a checklist with every decision written down. A fresh chat read them and picked up exactly where the last one stopped.

Starting fresh on purpose — The skill pack says this outright: starting a fresh conversation between skills is fine, because the files carry context forward. I didn't believe it until I tried it. The docs aren't paperwork for the judges. They're the memory.
The mistake was in the plan, not the code — On day two I did a timed run by hand, the way E. would. I found two problems. Neither one was a bug.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — The first was small. Sending an email takes 5 to 8 seconds while it builds the PDF, and the button didn't change. The code already blocked a double send, but it looked frozen. Now it says "Sending…" while it works.
The mistake was in the plan, not the code — The second was bigger. Every cafe had its own product list. E. has one menu, and any cafe can order anything on it.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — The agent traced it. The scope, the PRD and the spec all said "each cafe's standing list." The code did exactly what the plan said. Eight slices and a passing end-to-end test, all checking the plan faithfully, and the plan was wrong.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — Then we traced where the plan got it. Before I ever ran the skill pack, I wrote a planning brief with Claude. That brief looked at E.'s sample invoices, saw cookies on one cafe's invoice and not the others, and guessed that each cafe had its own list. An invoice shows what a cafe ordered that day, not what it's allowed to order. I brought that guess into the scope interview as if it were already decided, so the interview never asked E.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — I think that's the lesson I'm keeping. The interview checks your answers. It can't check what you bring in. Checking against the plan can't catch a mistake in the plan. Only using the thing the way the real person does could.

The mistake was in the plan, not the code — I had a choice. A data patch (put every product on every cafe's list) would have taken minutes. The full fix (one shared menu, drop the per-cafe table, correct the docs) took longer. I took the full fix, a week before the deadline, because E. is the user after the video, and a sixth product shouldn't have to be added four times forever.
The 20% leaks earlier now — I told the skill pack at 1-start what I wanted to learn: my builds land at about 80% of what I imagined, and I wanted to find where the other 20% leaks.

Failure mode 2: no idempotency key — The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing.

Failure mode 3: state that only exists in the context window — If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The payments service processes the refund, writes it to its ledger, and starts sending the response. The network hiccups. The agent's HTTP client hits its timeout and raises an error.

The gap between "decided" and "done" — From the agent's point of view, the call failed. From the payment service's point of view, it succeeded. The agent's loop sees an error, and the most natural thing for it to do is try again.

The gap between "decided" and "done" — The model reasoned perfectly. It picked the right action with the right arguments. Nothing about better prompting, a bigger model, or a smarter planner fixes this, because the failure happened after the reasoning was over.
Failure mode 1: treating a timeout as a "no" — The request reached it, succeeded, and the response was lost
Failure mode 2: no idempotency key — The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing.

Failure mode 3: state that only exists in the context window — If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The intent needs to be written to durable storage before execution, so that whatever process picks the work back up can see it.
Failure mode 4: no "outcome unknown" state — Confirmed: the downstream system acknowledged it

Failure mode 5: no reconciliation path — When an action lands in unknown, something has to go find out the truth: query the payment service by idempotency key or order ID, compare against the ledger, and then move the intent to confirmed or failed. That can be a background job, a scheduled check, or a human queue for high-value actions. What it can't be is the agent deciding "probably fine" or "probably failed" on its own.
The application owns the execution state — the key, the intent record, the status, the retry policy.

Build vs. integrate — If you already run payment or order flows with idempotency keys and outbox/ledger patterns, you mostly need to route agent actions through that same machinery instead of letting the agent call APIs directly. If you don't, that's the piece to build (or adopt) first, before giving an agent write access to anything that moves money or data.
all_paragraphs: Most agent demos have a happy path: the model picks a tool, the tool returns 200, the agent moves on. Production is different. In production, the tool call sometimes returns nothing at all.
That is where a correct decision turns into a wrong outcome.
Here is an illustrative scenario (not a real incident, but a very ordinary one).

An agent handles a support ticket and decides the customer is owed a refund. It calls POST /refunds. The payments service processes the refund, writes it to its ledger, and starts sending the response. The network hiccups. The agent's HTTP client hits its timeout and raises an error.
From the agent's point of view, the call failed. From the payment service's point of view, it succeeded. The agent's loop sees an error, and the most natural thing for it to do is try again.

The model reasoned perfectly. It picked the right action with the right arguments. Nothing about better prompting, a bigger model, or a smarter planner fixes this, because the failure happened after the reasoning was over.

A timeout tells you one thing: you didn't get an answer. It does not tell you the action didn't happen. Agent frameworks that wrap tool errors into "the tool failed, decide what to do next" collapse three different situations into one:

If the agent had sent an idempotency key, the second refund call would have been a no-op that returned the original result. The key has to be generated by the application before the first attempt and reused on every retry of that same intent:
The important part is where the key lives. If the model generates it, or if it's regenerated per attempt, it protects nothing.

If the record of "I already tried to refund order 4812" lives only in the conversation history, it disappears on a crash, a context truncation, or a restart of the worker. The intent needs to be written to durable storage before execution, so that whatever process picks the work back up can see it.
Unknown is the one that matters. It's the state that should block automatic retries and trigger reconciliation instead.

When an action lands in unknown, something has to go find out the truth: query the payment service by idempotency key or order ID, compare against the ledger, and then move the intent to confirmed or failed. That can be a background job, a scheduled check, or a human queue for high-value actions. What it can't be is the agent deciding "probably fine" or "probably failed" on its own.

Agent tool use is really remote procedure calls with an LLM choosing which procedure to call. Everything we already know about RPCs over unreliable networks still applies: idempotency, durable intent logs, explicit uncertainty, reconciliation.

"Try again" is a fine default for reads. For anything that changes state, it's only safe once you know the first attempt didn't land, or once the downstream system guarantees a retry can't double-apply.

If you already run payment or order flows with idempotency keys and outbox/ledger patterns, you mostly need to route agent actions through that same machinery instead of letting the agent call APIs directly. If you don't, that's the piece to build (or adopt) first, before giving an agent write access to anything that moves money or data.
How are you handling the "we don't know if it happened" case in your agent workflows? Are you blocking retries, reconciling, or escalating to a human?
